# Electricity in health-care facilities

## Key facts

## Overview

Electricity is needed to power the most basic services in health-care facilities, from lighting and communications to clean water supply. Reliable power is also crucial for the medical equipment necessary to safely manage childbirth or to ensure immunization as well as for undertaking most of the routine and emergency procedures. Reliable energy provision – particularly electricity – is a major enabler of universal health coverage. A number of clean and cost-effective energy solutions, such as based on solar photovoltaic systems, are available and rapidly deployable to electrify health-care facilities sustainably and increase their climate resiliency.

Yet, as highlighted in the report [Energizing health: accelerating electricity access in health-care facilities](/publications/i/item/9789240066960), close to 1 billion people in low- and lower-middle-income countries are estimated to be served by health-care facilities without reliable electricity access or with no electricity access at all. In low- and lower-middle-income countries of South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa, approximately 12% and 15% of health-care facilities, respectively, have no access to electricity whatsoever. There is a sharp urban–rural divide: urban health-care facilities often report more access to electricity and more reliable electricity than rural facilities in the same country.

Support, financing and investments need to be scaled up rapidly to accelerate health-care facility electrification. Other key actions include monitoring energy access in health-care facilities more systematically; providing the necessary resources to design and implement clean energy plans, tailored to the needs of the health sector; developing policy and finance schemes to unlock the potential of sustainable energy solutions, and to address the health sector needs.

## Global access status

Based on 27 low- and lower-middle-income countries that have national survey data on electrification status of health-care facilities for any year between 2015 and 2022, the following representative [findings](/publications/i/item/9789240066960) are found:

Hospitals tend to fare better than non-hospitals, such as primary health centres, in access to any electricity supply or reliable electricity supply. There is also an urban–rural divide: urban health-care facilities often report more access to any electricity and more reliable electricity access than rural facilities in the same country.

A closer look at other indicators that provide more detailed information on health-care facility electricity supply in subsets of countries show that generators are often not operational and that facilities are often underserved, with energy supply being insufficient to cover all the needs of the facility.

## Opportunities and benefits

Today, several solutions exist to electrify health-care facilities that were not available, or were too expensive, just a few years ago. For example, [decentralized sustainable energy solutions](/publications/i/item/9789240066960) based on solar photovoltaics and on batteries for storage are not only cost-effective and clean but rapidly deployable on site, without the need to wait for the arrival of the central grid.

Decentralized renewable energy systems dramatically increase climate resilience of health-care facilities, making them independent from the diesel supply needed for generators while reducing carbon and other polluting emissions.

Technical solutions and enabling delivery models exist and have been demonstrated to be successful. It is essential to scale up investments and accelerate action to ensure reliable electricity to all health centres, including in remote and rural areas.

The World Bank estimates that [US$ 4.9 billion](/publications/i/item/9789240066960) is urgently needed to bring health-care facilities in 63 low- and middle-income countries up to a minimal or intermediate level of electrification to ensure that all the essential health services are covered.

Health is a human right and a public good. Significant policy changes and increased support are necessary to ensure that all health-care facilities have reliable electricity supply to address health inequities, achieve the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development including universal health coverage, and mitigate climate change.

## WHO response

WHO supports countries ensure a reliable supply of electricity for health-care facilities by providing the knowledge and tools to a) understand the energy access situation and the energy needs of health-care facilities in their country, b) build the institutional capacity to identify the most suitable energy solutions to meet their needs, c) build an enabling framework to accelerate health-care facility electrification, and d) support high-level advocacy, coordination and mobilization of adequate resources for impact on the ground.

### Data gathering, analysis and harmonization

Establishing baselines and measuring progress is an essential step to identify gaps and priority needs for the allocation of limited resources. Building on the [WHO health-care facility electrification database,](/data/gho/data/themes/database-on-electrification-of-health-care-facilities) WHO collects and analyzes data regarding the energy status of health infrastructure to measure progress on access to electricity as well as on access to reliable electricity, among other indicators.

### Knowledge creation

WHO gathers lessons and good practices on electrification of health-care facilities. It identifies and consolidates key insights on successful and innovative policies, regulations, financing instruments, delivery models and support measures with countries as well as to identify priority actions to accelerate health-care facility electrification. Guidance and support to countries are provided via direct technical assistance as well as through the dissemination of reports and best practices, like those included in the [Energizing health: accelerating electricity access in health-care facilities](/publications/i/item/9789240066960) report.

### **Technical support for country action**

WHO provides direct technical support to countries on techno-economic analyses for electrification of health-care facilities through decentralized renewable energies.

This activity includes support for:

### **Capacity building**

WHO support countries on strengthening professional capacity of health workers at different levels, from central governments to local health centres. This activity aims to increase the ability of the local health sector to design, implement and maintain health-care facility electrification programmes. WHO also works with local stakeholders to strengthen the capacity of health-care facility staff to properly use the facility energy systems and undertake the basic maintenance.

### **Building the enabling environment**

WHO facilitates multisector cooperation and coordinated action among health and energy stakeholders to maximize impact and leverage on synergies on the ground. In this framework, WHO serves as Secretariat of the [Health and Energy Platform of Action (HEPA)](https://www.who.int/initiatives/health-and-energy-platform-of-action) and plays a crucial role in multi-stakeholder platforms relevant for health and energy, such as the climate change conferences of parties (COPs), UN Energy, and Sustainable Development Goal 7 progress tracking.

No. A-110018/01/2021-CAQM Dated: 29.09.2026 Subject: Directions under Section 12 of the Commission for Air Quality Management in National Capital Region and Adjoining Areas Act, 2021 – Revised Schedule of the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) for NCR 1. WHEREAS, high levels of air pollution in the National Capital Region (NCR), particularly episodic increases during periods of adverse meteorological conditions, have been a matter of serious concern, and the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) was initially notified by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change in January, 2017, pursuant to the directions of the Hon’ble Supreme Court, to provide for graded measures corresponding to different levels of air quality; 2. WHEREAS, the Commission for Air Quality Management in National Capital Region and Adjoining Areas (hereinafter referred to as “the Commission”) has been constituted under the Commission for Air Quality Management in National Capital Region and Adjoining Areas Act, 2021 (hereinafter referred to as “the Act”) and Section 12 of the Act empowers the Commission to take such measures and issue such directions as it considers necessary or expedient for the purpose of protecting and improving the quality of air in the National Capital Region and Adjoining Areas; 3. WHEREAS, GRAP provides for a graded framework of preventive, restrictive and other measures for implementation at different levels of air Direction No. 104 quality, with a view to preventing further deterioration of air quality, particularly during periods of adverse meteorological conditions; 4. WHEREAS, having regard to experience gained in its implementation, developments in measures for prevention, control and abatement of air pollution and the need for timely preventive action, the GRAP Schedule has undergone review and revision from time to time, while retaining its underlying graded response framework; 5. WHEREAS, the Hon’ble Supreme Court, in W.P.(C) No. 13029 of 1985, M.C. Mehta v. Union of India & Ors., vide Order dated 12.12.2024, approved the recommendations of the Sub-Committee on GRAP, as placed before it by the Commission, and directed implementation of the modified GRAP Schedule. Further, the Hon’ble Supreme Court vide Order dated 17.02.2025, reiterated that the Commission will implement the comprehensive GRAP Schedule as approved by it on 12.12.2024. Thereafter, the Hon’ble Supreme Court vide its Order dated 19.11.2025, while accepting the suggestions of the Commission for advancing certain measures from higher stages of GRAP to earlier stages, observed, inter alia, that any pro-active action by the Commission aimed at reducing air pollution levels would always be welcome; 6. WHEREAS, while placing proposals for revision of the GRAP Schedule before the Hon’ble Supreme Court in November, 2025, the Commission had, inter alia, highlighted that GRAP measures are regularly reviewed from time to time and additional measures are undertaken, as required; and, upon consideration of the proposals so placed, certain measures under the higher stages of GRAP were advanced to earlier stages and accordingly incorporated in the GRAP Schedule issued on 21.11.2025; 7. WHEREAS, GRAP is essentially a dynamic and graded response mechanism intended to enable timely preventive and restrictive actions Direction No. 104 commensurate with the prevailing and anticipated air quality conditions. Its effective implementation, therefore, requires periodic consideration of the measures under its respective stages, having regard to experience gained in implementation, prevailing air quality scenario, developments in pollution control measures and other relevant considerations; 8. WHEREAS, experience gained in implementation of the extant GRAP Schedule and the measures undertaken from time to time for prevention, control and abatement of air pollution in the NCR have been considered with a view to ensure that the measures under the respective stages remain appropriately aligned with the prevailing requirements; 9. WHEREAS, considering the aforesaid aspects, the Sub-Committee for operationalization of the GRAP had detailed deliberations, reviewed the extant GRAP Schedule and proposed certain measures under the respective stages of GRAP that require suitable revision and rationalisation so as to further improve the effectiveness and responsiveness of the graded response mechanism and facilitate timely action for prevention and control of air pollution in the NCR; 10. WHEREAS, the Commission is, accordingly, of the view that it is appropriate and necessary, in the interest of effective implementation of GRAP and prevention of further deterioration of air quality in the NCR, to issue a suitably revised GRAP Schedule, incorporating the measures considered necessary under its respective stages, while retaining the overall graded response framework of GRAP; 11. NOW, THEREFORE, in exercise of the powers conferred under Section 12 of the Commission for Air Quality Management in National Capital Region and Adjoining Areas Act, 2021, the Commission hereby issues the revised Schedule of the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) for NCR, as annexed to this Direction, with immediate effect. Direction No. 104 12. The revised Schedule shall henceforth govern the implementation of GRAP in the NCR. The measures prescribed under the respective stages of GRAP shall be applicable as and when the respective stage is invoked through appropriate orders. 13. The Government of NCT of Delhi, Governments of the NCR States, concerned Ministries/ Departments of the Central Government, NCR State Pollution Control Boards/ DPCC, Urban Local Bodies, Development Authorities and all other authorities/ agencies concerned shall, within their respective jurisdictions, ensure implementation and enforcement of the measures applicable under the respective stages of GRAP, as and when invoked. 14. All agencies, project proponents, industries, commercial establishments, other entities and persons concerned shall comply with the measures applicable to them under the respective stages of the GRAP Schedule, upon invocation thereof. 15. The Schedule annexed hereto shall form an integral part of this Direction. (Tarun Kumar Pithode) Member Secretary Email: mscaqm-moefcc@gov.in To: 1. The Chairperson and all Members (including Associate Members), CAQM (Tarun Kumar Pithode) Member Secretary COMMISSION FOR AIR QUALITY MANAGEMENT IN NATIONAL CAPITAL REGION AND ADJOINING AREAS GRADED RESPONSE ACTION PLAN (GRAP) FOR THE NATIONAL CAPITAL REGION (NCR) (Revision: 29.09.2026) 1. The GRAP for the entire NCR has been classified under 4 different stages of adverse air quality in Delhi viz. Stage – I ‘Poor’ (AQI 201 – 300), Stage – II ‘Very Poor (AQI 301-400), Stage – III ‘Severe’ (AQI 401-450) and Stage – IV ‘Severe +’ (AQI >450) respectively. 2. Based on the dynamic model and weather/ meteorological forecast by IMD / IITM on a day-to-day basis, actions under Stages I, II, III and IV of the GRAP shall be invoked in advance of the AQI of Delhi reaching to the projected levels of that stage, also provided that the higher projected AQI levels are likely to sustain for longer period. 3. Even if the AQI forecast does not indicate the AQI of Delhi to be breaching a particular threshold and under extreme meteorological conditions or due to any episodic event the AQI breaches the threshold, that particular stage of the GRAP shall be invoked with immediate effect in respect of actions / measures that can be invoked immediately. 4. Restrictive actions undertaken as per previous stages shall be continued, in addition to the air pollution stage under which the restrictive actions are envisaged to be taken. For example, restrictive actions under the Stage III category, whenever invoked, shall be in addition to those under Stage I and II respectively and so on and so forth. 5. The Sub-Committee on GRAP constituted by the Commission shall meet frequently to plan for advance action and issue necessary orders for invoking various provisions of the GRAP, based on the prevalent air quality and the AQI forecast to be provided by IMD from time to time. The Sub-Committee shall also review the actions taken by various agencies responsible towards effective implementation of the GRAP. 6. The Chief Secretaries of NCR States and GNCTD shall frequently review the actions and implementation of the GRAP especially when the air quality falls or is likely to fall in the ‘Severe’ or ‘Severe +’ category (Stage III and beyond). 7. The Commission may decide upon any exceptions and additional measures to the schedule of the GRAP, under different air pollution categories i.e., Stages I to IV, as per the prevalent AQI and weather forecast. Schedule under the GRAP for NCR Stage I – ‘Poor’ Air Quality (DELHI AQI ranging between 201-300) Actions Agencies responsible / Implementing Agencies 1. Ensure proper implementation of Directions/ Rules/ Guidelines for enforcement of dust mitigation measures (C&D materials & waste are properly stored & duly covered, transportation of C&D materials/ waste only in covered vehicles, yardsticks for anti-smog guns, water sprinkling etc.) in Construction and Demolition (C&D) activities and sound environmental management of C&D waste. 2. Ensure strict compliance of Direction Nos. 11-18 dated 11.06.2021 and do not permit C&D activities in respect of such C&D projects with plot size equal to or more than 500 sqm, which are not registered on the ‘web portal’ of the respective State / GNCTD and / or which do not fulfil the other requirements as per the above noted statutory Directions, for remote monitoring of dust mitigation measures. - Chairpersons/ Member Secretaries – CPCB, DPCC, SPCBs (NCR). - Commissioners / Chief Engineers of Urban Local Bodies in Delhi-NCR towns. - Construction agencies and plot owners (both public & private). 3. Ensure regular lifting of Municipal Solid Waste (MSW), C&D waste, Industrial and Hazardous waste from dedicated dump sites/ industrial areas and ensure that no waste is dumped illegally in open land areas. - Chairpersons/ Member Secretaries – CPCB, DPCC, SPCBs (NCR). - Commissioners / Chief Engineers of Urban Local Bodies in Delhi-NCR towns. - DMs/ DCs of respective districts in NCR. - All land-owning agencies. - Construction agencies (both public & private). 4. Carry out periodic mechanized sweeping and water sprinkling on roads and ensure scientific disposal of the dust collected in designated sites/landfills. - Commissioners / Chief Engineers of Urban Local Bodies in Delhi-NCR towns. - Chief Executives of all road owning and maintaining agencies. 5. Intensify use of anti-smog guns, water sprinkling and dust suppression measures in road construction / widening / repair projects and maintenance activities. - All road owning / maintenance agencies in NCR. 6. Strictly enforce prohibition on open burning of bio-mass and municipal solid waste. Impose maximum EC upon violations in accordance with Hon’ble NGT’s orders dated 04.12.2014 and 28.04.2015 in OA 21/2014. 7. Strict vigil to ensure that there are no burning incidents in the landfill sites / dumpsites. - Chairpersons/ Member Secretaries – CPCB, DPCC, SPCBs (NCR). - Commissioners / Chief Engineers of Urban Local Bodies in Delhi-NCR towns. - All land-owning agencies. 8. Synchronize traffic movements and deploy adequate personnel at all identified corridors with heavy traffic, congestion points/ intersections for smooth flow of traffic. - Commissioner or Head of Traffic Police in Delhi and NCR towns. 9. Strict vigilance and enforcement of PUC norms for vehicles and stop visibly polluting vehicles by impounding and / or levying maximum penalty. - Commissioner or Head of Transport Department of Delhi and NCR States - Commissioner or Head of Traffic Police of Delhi and NCR towns. 10. Strictly enforce the Hon’ble Supreme Court’s order regarding diversion of non- destined truck traffic for Delhi, through Eastern and Western Peripheral Expressways. - Head of Traffic Police of Delhi and NCR towns. - DMs / Dy Commissioners of NCT of Delhi / NCR towns. - Municipal Commissioner of Corporations of NCT of Delhi and NCR towns. 11. Strictly enforce NGT / Hon’ble Supreme Court orders regarding ban on plying of overaged diesel / petrol vehicles and other restrictions as per extant statutes. - Commissioner or Head of Transport Department of Delhi and NCR States - Commissioner or Head of Traffic Police of Delhi and NCR towns. 12. Intensify inspection of industries including in non-conforming areas and ensure strict penal/ legal action against non-compliant and illegal units. 13. Strictly enforce all pollution control regulations in industries, brick kilns, hot mix plants etc. in NCR - strict compliance of the prescribed emission standards and use of approved fuels only. - Chairpersons/ Member Secretaries – CPCB, DPCC, SPCBs (NCR). - District Magistrates / Deputy Commissioners of NCT of Delhi / NCR States. - Commissioners of Urban Local Bodies in Delhi and NCR towns. 14. Strictly enforce emission norms in thermal power plants and penal/ legal action be taken against non-compliance. - Plant in- charge of Power Plants located within 300 km radius of Delhi. - Chairpersons/ Member Secretaries – CPCB, DPCC, SPCBs (NCR). 15. Strictly enforce orders of Hon’ble Courts / Tribunal regarding firecrackers. - Commissioner of Police of Delhi & IG / DIG / SP of NCR towns or Officer In Charge of Licensing. - DMs/ DCs/SSPs of respective districts in NCR. - Chief Controller of Explosives, Petroleum and Explosive Safety Organizations (PESO). 16. DISCOMs to minimise power supply interruptions in NCR. - Head of Power distribution companies in Delhi-NCR. 17. Ensure that diesel generator sets are not used as regular source of power supply. 18. Strictly implement the regulated operations of DG sets across all sectors in the NCR including Industrial, Commercial, Residential etc. in accordance with Direction No. 76 dated 29.09.2023 with amendments, if any. Capacity Range of DG sets System to be adopted for control of emissions Regulation s for use Power generating sets of all capacities running on LPG/ Natural Gas/Bio-gas/ Propane/Butane None No restrictions Power generating sets up to 800 kW (1000 kVA) capacity to standards as per MoEFCC notification No. GSR 804 (E) dated 03.11.2022 None No restrictions. DG sets to older specifications / standards 800 kW (1000 kVA) and above Any emission control system/mechan ism, however subject to compliance of the prescribed emission standards in Direction no. 76 No restrictions 41 kW (51 kVA) to less than 800 kW (1000 kVA) Dual fuel mode OR Retro-fitted ECDs through certified agencies No restrictions 19 kW (23 kVA) to less than 41 kW (51 kVA) Dual fuel mode No restrictions Note: DG Sets not working in a dual fuel mode, only owing to non-availability of gas infrastructu re and supply, shall be permitted only for prescribed emergency services. * - Chairpersons/ Member Secretaries – CPCB, DPCC, SPCBs (NCR). - Commissioners / Chief Engineers of Urban Local Bodies in Delhi-NCR towns. - District Magistrates / Deputy Commissioners of NCR States and GNCTD. Portable DG sets below 19kW (23 kVA) Presently no specific means of emission control are available in this category / capacity range of DG sets. Not to be generally permitted. Permitted only for the prescribed emergency services. * Emergency services: (i) Only for operating elevators / Escalators / travelators. (ii) Medical Services (Hospital / Nursing Home/ Health care facilities). (iii) Railway Services / Railway Stations. (iv) Metro Rail Corporation & MRTS Services. (v) Airports and Inter-State Bus Terminals. (vi) Sewage Treatment Plants. (vii) Water pumping Stations. (viii) Projects related to national security, defence & of national importance. (ix) Telecommunications and IT/ data services. 19. Do not permit inter-city/ inter-state buses from any city/ town of the states of Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan and also from the adjoining states of Punjab, Himachal Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Uttarakhand and J&K, other than EV / CNG / BS-VI Diesel, to ply in Delhi- NCR. - State Governments in NCR and GNCTD. - Transport Commissioners, GNCTD/ NCR States - Commissioner of Police / Head of Traffic Police of Delhi and NCR towns. 20. Strictly enforce the extant ban on use of coal / firewood as fuel in Tandoors in Hotels, Restaurants and open eateries and ensure use of only electricity / gas-based / clean fuel - based appliances in these establishments. - Commissioners / Chief Engineers of Urban Local Bodies in Delhi-NCR towns. - Chairpersons/ Member Secretaries – CPCB, DPCC, SPCBs (NCR). 21. Undertake intensive Information, Education and Communication (IEC) activities through print, electronic and social media, bulk SMS etc. including issuing alerts to citizens about Do’s and Don’ts for minimizing polluting activities. 22. Mobile Apps to be used to inform people about the pollution levels and contact details of control room to enable them to report polluting activities / sources to the concerned authorities and inform them about actions that would be taken by Government. - ACS/ Pr. Secretary/ Secretary, Dept. of Environment, GNCTD and NCR States. - Chairpersons/ Member Secretaries – CPCB, DPCC, SPCBs (NCR). 23. Ensure quick actions for redressal of complaints on 311 App, Green Delhi App, SAMEER App, other such Apps and social media platforms to curb polluting activities. - Head of Urban Local Bodies in NCR towns. - Chairpersons/ Member Secretaries – CPCB, DPCC, SPCBs (NCR). - Construction agencies, land owning agencies, Development agencies, Road owning agencies and all other concerned implementing agencies. 24. Encourage offices to start unified commute for employees to reduce traffic on road. - State Governments in NCR and GNCTD. 25. Augment public transport services through CNG/ electric buses, metro and RRTS services by inducting additional fleet and increasing the frequency of service. Introduce differential rates to encourage off – peak travel. - GNCTD and NCR State Governments. - Principal Secretary, Department of Transport. of NCT of Delhi and NCR State Govts. - Delhi Transport Corporation (DTC). - State Transport Corporations in NCR towns. - Delhi Integrated Multi – Model Transit System Ltd. (DIMTS). - Metro Rail Corporations (DMRC, NMRC, GMRL). - National Capital Region Transport Corporation (NCRTC). CITIZEN CHARTER • Check AQI from SAMEER App and stage of GRAP in force from CAQM website. • Keep engines of your vehicles properly tuned. • Maintain proper tyre pressure in vehicles. • Keep PUC certificates of your vehicles up to date. • Do not idle your vehicle, also turn off the engine at red lights. • Do not ply end-of-life / visibly polluting diesel or petrol vehicles. • Prefer public transport or pooling of vehicles for commuting. • Prefer EVs to control vehicular pollution. Ensure segregation and proper disposal of municipal solid waste. • Do not litter / dispose waste, garbage in open spaces. • Ensure disposal of waste only in designated collection points provided by municipal authorities especially in markets and public places. • Ensure immediate removal of C&D waste and compliances of dust mitigation measures. • Plant more trees and cover open spaces with grass and shrubs. • Avoid using DG sets except for essential activities. • Celebrate festivals in an eco-friendly manner – avoid firecrackers. • Report air polluting activities through 311 App, Green Delhi App, SAMEER App etc. • Participate in Information Education and Communication (IEC) activities and spread awareness about air pollution mitigation measures among fellow citizens through various means including social media channels. Stage II – ‘Very Poor’ Air Quality (DELHI AQI ranging between 301-400) Actions Agencies responsible / Implementing Agencies 1. Carry out mechanical/ vacuum sweeping along with water sprinkling of the identified roads on a daily basis preferably during night or early morning hours. Enhance the number of shifts / hours of deployment of such machines to further intensify mechanised sweeping and ensure proper disposal of the collected dust in designated sites/ landfills. 2. Ensure daily water sprinkling along with dust suppressants, before peak traffic hours, on roads and right of ways especially at heavy traffic corridors and other congestion points. - Commissioners / Chief Engineers of Urban Local Bodies in Delhi-NCR towns - Chief Executives of all road owning and maintaining agencies. - Commissioner of Traffic Police of Delhi & NCR towns to identify roads with heavy traffic and provide information to respective Municipal Commissioners / Heads of Municipal Bodies. 3. Ensure focussed and targeted actions for abatement of air pollution in all identified hotspots in Delhi-NCR. Intensify remedial measures for the predominant sector(s) contributing to adverse air quality in each of such hotspots. - State Govts. in NCR and GNCTD. - Chairpersons/ Member Secretaries – CPCB, DPCC, SPCBs (NCR). - Commissioners / Chief Engineers of Urban Local Bodies in Delhi and NCR towns. 4. Intensify inspections for strict enforcement of dust control measures at C&D sites. - Chairpersons/ Member Secretaries – CPCB, DPCC, SPCBs (NCR). - Commissioners / Chief Engineers of Urban Local Bodies in Delhi and NCR towns. 5. Enhance vehicle parking fees to discourage private transport. - Principal Secretary, Urban Local Bodies of NCR States and GNCTD. - Commissioners of Urban Local Bodies in Delhi and NCR towns. 6. Resident Welfare Associations (RWAs) to necessarily provide electric heaters (with provision of electricity supply / point) to staff engaged in security, sanitation, horticulture and other miscellaneous services to avoid open biomass/ MSW burning during winters. - Resident Welfare Associations. - Municipal Commissioners / Heads of Municipal Bodies in Delhi and NCR towns. 7. (i) GNCTD and NCR State Governments to stagger timings for public offices and municipal bodies in the National Capital Territory of Delhi and the districts of Gurugram, Faridabad, Ghaziabad and Gautam Buddha Nagar. (ii) State Governments may take a decision to stagger timings for public offices and municipal bodies in other areas of NCR. - GNCTD and NCR State Governments. - NCR State Governments. 8. Central Government may take a decision on staggering of timings of Central Government offices in Delhi – NCR. - Central Government CITIZEN CHARTER • People to use public transport and minimize use of personal vehicles. • Use technology and take less congested route even if slightly longer. • Ensure proper parking, lane driving and clearance to pedestrian footpaths. • Regularly replace air filters at recommended intervals in your vehicles. • Avoid dust generating construction activities during the months of October to January. • Ensure cleaning of kitchen chimney filters at regular intervals. • Avoid outdoor smoke generating cooking and heating activities in residential areas and public spaces. • Avoid accumulation and open burning of solid waste and biomass. • People, whose positions allow working from home, may work from home. Stage III – ‘Severe’ Air Quality (DELHI AQI ranging between 401-450) Actions Agencies responsible / Implementing Agencies 1. Construction & Demolition activities: (i) Enforce strict restrictions on the following categories of dust generating/ air pollution causing construction and demolition (C&D) activities in the entire NCR: • Earthwork for excavation and filling including boring & drilling works. • Piling works. • All demolition works. • Laying of sewer line, water line, drainage and electric cabling etc. by open trench system. • Brick / masonry works. • Operation of RMC batching plant. • Major welding and gas-cutting operations. Minor welding activities for MEP works (Mechanical, Electrical and Plumbing) to be, however, permitted. • Painting, polishing and varnishing works etc. • Cement, Plaster / other coatings, except for minor indoor repairs / maintenance. • Cutting / grinding and fixing of tiles, stones and other flooring materials, except for minor indoor repairs/maintenance. • Road construction activities and major repairs. Repairing of potholes shall, however, be permitted. • Transfer, loading / unloading of dust generating materials like cement, fly-ash, bricks, sand, murram, pebbles, crushed stone etc. anywhere within / outside the project sites. - NCR State Governments and GNCTD - Chairpersons/ Member Secretaries – CPCB, DPCC, SPCBs (NCR). - Commissioners / Chief Engineers of Urban Local Bodies in Delhi and NCR towns. - All construction agencies and plot owners (both public & private). • Movement of vehicles carrying construction materials or C&D waste on unpaved roads. (ii) All construction related activities, other than those listed under 1(i) above, which are relatively less polluting / less dust generating shall be permitted to be continued in the NCR, subject to strict compliance of the C&D Waste Management Rules, dust prevention/ control norms including compliance with the directions of the Commission issued from time to time. (iii) All C&D related activities, including those under 1(i) above, shall be continued to be permitted only for the following categories of projects, however subject to strict compliance of the C&D Waste Management Rules, dust prevention/ control norms including compliance with the directions of the Commission issued from time to time: a) Projects for Railway services and stations b) Projects for Metro Rail Services and stations c) Airports and Inter State Bus Terminals d) National security/ defence related activities/ projects of national importance; e) Hospitals/ health care facilities f) Linear public projects such as highways, roads, flyovers, over bridges, power transmission/ distribution, pipelines, tele-communication services etc. g) Sanitation projects like sewage treatment plants and water supply projects etc. h) Ancillary activities, specific to and supplementing the above project categories. 2. Close down operations of stone crushers in the entire NCR. - Chairpersons/ Member Secretaries – CPCB, DPCC, SPCBs (NCR). - Commissioner of Police - Delhi and DG of Police of NCR States. - District Magistrates / Deputy Commissioners of respective districts in Delhi and NCR States. 3. Close down all mining and associated activities in the entire NCR. - Chairpersons/ Member Secretaries – CPCB, DPCC, SPCBs (NCR). - Commissioner of Police - Delhi and DG of Police of NCR States. - District Magistrates / Deputy Commissioners of respective districts in NCR. 4. NCR State Govts. / GNCTD to impose strict restrictions on plying of BS III petrol and BS IV diesel or below standard Light Motor Vehicles (LMVs) (4 wheelers) in Delhi and in the High Vehicle Density (HVD) districts of Gurugram, Faridabad, Sonipat, Ghaziabad and Gautam Budha Nagar. Note: Persons with Disabilities shall be permitted to ply BS – III Petrol / BS – IV Diesel LMVs, provided that these are specifically adopted for them and are run only for their personal use. - State Governments in NCR and GNCTD. - Transport Commissioners, GNCTD/ NCR States - Commissioner of Police / Head of Traffic Police of Delhi and NCR towns. 5. GNCTD to impose strict restrictions on plying of Delhi - registered diesel operated BS-IV and below standard Medium Goods Vehicles (MGVs), in Delhi. - State Governments in NCR and GNCTD. - Transport Commissioners, GNCTD/ NCR States - Commissioner of Police / Head of Traffic Police of Delhi and NCR towns. 6. GNCTD to not permit diesel operated BS-IV and below standard MGVs, registered outside Delhi, to enter Delhi. - State Governments in NCR and GNCTD. - Transport Commissioners, GNCTD/ NCR States - Commissioners / Head of Urban Local Bodies in Delhi-NCR towns. - Commissioner of Police / Head of Traffic Police of Delhi and NCR towns. 7. GNCTD to not permit diesel operated BS-IV and below standard Light Goods Vehicles (LGVs), registered outside Delhi, to enter Delhi. - State Governments in NCR and GNCTD. - Transport Commissioners, GNCTD/ NCR States - Commissioners / Head of Urban Local Bodies in Delhi-NCR towns. - Commissioner of Police / Head of Traffic Police of Delhi and NCR towns. 8. (i) State Govts. in the NCR and the GNCTD to mandatorily conduct classes in schools for children up to class V in a “Hybrid” mode i.e., both in physical and online mode (wherever online mode is feasible) in the territorial jurisdiction of the NCT of Delhi and in the districts of Gurugram, Faridabad, Ghaziabad and Gautam Buddha Nagar. (ii) The NCR State Governments may also consider conducting classes for students up to Class V in a “Hybrid” mode as above in other areas in NCR. Note: The option to exercise the online mode of education, wherever available, shall vest with the students and their guardians. - State Governments of NCR & GNCTD. - NCR State Governments. 9. NCR State Governments / GNCTD to take a decision on allowing public, municipal and private offices to work on 50% strength and the rest to work from home. - State Governments of NCR & GNCTD. 10. Central Government may take appropriate decision on permitting work from home for employees in Central Government offices. - Central Government (DoPT). CITIZEN CHARTER • Walk or use cycles for small distances. • Choose a cleaner transport mode to commute. • Combine short journeys and reduce trips. • Postpone private gatherings that increase traffic and outdoor exposure. • Do not use coal and wood for heating purpose. • House owners may also provide electric heaters to security/other staff employed by them to avoid open burning of biomass / wood / MSW. • Follow hybrid mode for primary schools and work-from-home when instructed. Stage IV – ‘Severe +’ Air Quality (DELHI AQI > 450) Actions Agencies responsible / Implementing Agencies 1. Stop entry of trucks i.e. Heavy Goods Vehicles (HGVs) into Delhi. All LNG/ CNG / Electric/ BS-VI diesel trucks shall, however, be permitted to enter Delhi. - State Governments of NCR & GNCTD. - Transport Commissioners, GNCTD/ NCR States - Commissioners / Head of Urban Local Bodies in Delhi-NCR towns. - Commissioner of Police / Head of Traffic Police of Delhi and NCR towns. 2. Enforce strict ban on plying of Delhi - registered diesel operated BS-IV and below standard HGVs in Delhi. All LNG/ CNG / Electric/ BS-VI diesel trucks shall, however, be permitted to enter Delhi. - State Governments of NCR & GNCTD. - Transport Commissioners, GNCTD/ NCR States. - Commissioner of Police / Head of Traffic Police of Delhi and NCR towns. 3. Ban C&D activities, as in the GRAP Stage- III, also for linear public projects such as highways, roads, flyovers, overbridges, power transmission, pipelines, tele-communication etc. - Chairpersons/ Member Secretaries – CPCB, DPCC, SPCBs (NCR). - Commissioners / Chief Engineers of Urban Local Bodies in Delhi - NCR towns. - Nodal Officers of road owning agencies (Dust Control and Management Cells). 4. (i) State Govts. in the NCR and the GNCTD to mandatorily conduct classes in schools for children even for higher classes i.e. from class VI to IX and XI in a “Hybrid” mode i.e., both in physical and online mode (wherever online mode is feasible) in the territorial jurisdiction of the NCT of Delhi and in the districts of Gurugram, Faridabad, Ghaziabad and Gautam Buddha Nagar. (ii) The NCR State Governments may also consider conducting classes for students as - State Governments of NCR & GNCTD. - NCR State Governments. above in a “Hybrid” mode in other areas in NCR. Note: The option to exercise the online mode of education, wherever available, shall vest with the students and their guardians. 5. State Governments may consider additional emergency measures like closure of colleges/ educational institutions and closure of non-emergency commercial activities, permitting running of vehicles on odd-even basis of registration numbers etc. - State Governments of NCR & GNCTD. CITIZEN CHARTER • Citizens are advised to limit non-essential outdoor activity. • Children, pregnant women, elderly and those with respiratory, cardiovascular, cerebrovascular or other chronic diseases to avoid outdoor activities and stay indoors, as much as possible. If required to move outdoors, they are advised to wear mask. • Follow hybrid mode for schools and restrictions on other activities as and when instructed. ********

searches.answer: The sources indicate that flooding in Nepal has caused disruptions, including the stranding of more than 100 foreign trekkers after hiking trails were swept away. The World Bank documents highlight risks to Nepal's development, including potential fuel supply disruptions and infrastructure damage from floods, which could prolong disruptions to transport, trade, tourism, hydropower generation, and private sector activity. There is no specific mention of a fuel supply disruption in the town context, but the general theme of flood-related disruptions is consistent across the sources.

results.title: Nepal Development Update
results.content: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY W O R L D B A N K G R O U P | 9 NEPAL DEVELOPMENT UPDATE | OCTOBER 2026 The risks to the outlook are tilted to the downside, with the pace and design of post-flood recovery representing a key domestic uncertainty. Prolonged conflict in the Middle East could reduce tourism and remittance inflows, weaken consumption and services activity, and dampen overall growth, while disruptions to fertilizer and fuel supplies could raise production costs and constrain agricultural output, investment, and broader economic activity. Domestically, delays in relief, reconstruction, and restoration of flood-damaged infrastructure could prolong disruptions to transport, trade, tourism, hydropower generation, and private sector activity, while the high share of uninsured assets could slow [...] B.4 RISKS AND CHALLENGES The risks to the outlook are tilted to the downside. Key downside risks include a prolonged conflict in the Middle East, which could reduce tourist arrivals and remittance inflows, dampen consumption and services activity, and slow overall growth. Disruptions in fertilizer imports could raise production costs and reduce agricultural output, while fuel supply constraints could weigh on investment and economic activity more broadly. Domestically, the main risks include delays in relief, reconstruction, and restoration of infrastructure damaged by the August 2026 flood. This could prolong disruptions to transport, trade, tourism, hydropower generation, and private sector activity. The high share of uninsured assets could further constrain the pace of recovery and [...] PRINCIPLE 2. Build redundancy into critical infrastructure and networks The flood demonstrated the risks created when communities and markets depend on a limited number of transports, energy or communications links. Future infrastructure planning should therefore consider redundancy and alternative connections, so that the failure of a single road, bridge, transmission line or other critical asset does not isolate communities or disrupt essential services across a much larger area. This is not simply about making individual infrastructure stronger. It is about designing systems that can continue to function when individual assets fail.

Sislen (Division Director for Maldives, Nepal, and Sri Lanka), Shabih Ali Mohib (Practice Manager, ESAC1), S. Amer Ahmed (Manager, Operations), and Arvind Nair (Lead Country Economist, ESAC1). Agricultural sector growth slowed to 1.6 percent, from 3.0 percent in FY25, mainly due to a 4.2 percent contraction in paddy production. Adverse weather conditions, including drought during the peak paddy transplantation period in Madhesh, and excessive rainfall during the October 2025 harvest, weighed on production. In contrast, industrial sector growth accelerated to 5.7 percent, from 3.3 percent in FY25, driven by a 21 percent expansion in electricity generation and higher hydropower capacity. Services growth moderated slightly to 4.2 percent, from 4.4 percent, as stronger domestic trade and financial and insurance services were offset by slower growth in transportation and accommodation and food services.
Inflation declined to a record low of 3.1 percent, well below the central bank’s 5 percent ceiling. This was largely due to lower food inflation, which supported household purchasing power. Non-food inflation increased marginally, partly reflecting higher fuel and transportation prices amid the Middle East conflict. The current account surplus doubled to a record of 14.0 percent of GDP, supported by remittance inflows of 35.8 percent of GDP, which offset a widening trade deficit. Remittances increased despite a 19.6 percent decline in new international migrant workers, reflecting higher remittances per worker, destination diversification, Nepali Rupee depreciation against the US dollar, and greater use of formal and digital channels. The trade deficit widened as imports increased faster than exports, driven by higher imports of intermediate goods and higher global fuel prices. Exports of goods and services also increased, supported by higher refined soybean oil re-exports to India and growth in professional and management consulting and ICT services. The strong external position supported further accumulation of foreign exchange reserves, which reached USD 25.3 billion by end FY26, equivalent to 19.6 months of imports of goods and services, up from 15.4 months in FY25 and more than twice the Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB)’s 7-month regulatory minimum.
Contained inflation and favorable liquidity environment provided room for an accommodative monetary policy stance, but credit growth remained subdued. The NRB reduced the policy rate to 4.25 percent and narrowed the interest rate corridor amid persistent excess liquidity in FY26. Lower policy and market rates contributed to declines in deposit and lending interest rates, while record remittance inflows and foreign exchange purchases supported strong banking deposit growth. Despite historically low lending interest rates and additional measures to encourage credit expansion, private sector credit increased only marginally to 95.9 percent of GDP in FY26 from 95.7 percent in FY25, reflecting continued weakness in domestic demand. At the same time, financial sector asset quality deteriorated, with the gross Non-performing Loan (NPL) ratio reaching a record of 5.7 percent by mid-July 2026, with deterioration observed across all major categories of financial institutions. Rising NPLs increased loan-loss provisions by 0.1 percentage point of GDP to 1.2 percent, contributing, together with lower net interest income, to a modest decline in financial sector net profits. Regulatory forbearance measures helped cushion the impact of asset-quality deterioration. Capital buffers remained resilient, with the aggregate Capital Adequacy Ratio (CAR) at 12.8 percent at end-FY26, above the 11 percent regulatory minimum. Nepal’s continued presence on the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) grey list increases cross-border transaction and compliance costs.
The fiscal deficit and debt increased marginally, as a slight decline in revenues was offset partly by continued challenges in capital expenditure execution. The fiscal deficit widened marginally to 1.7 percent of GDP in FY26 from 1.6 percent in FY25, as revenue and grants declined faster than expenditure. Revenue and grants fell by 0.3 percentage point of GDP to 19.4 percent, mainly due to lower income tax and non-tax revenue, partly offset by higher VAT and excise receipts. Total expenditure declined slightly to 21.1 percent of GDP, as lower capital spending more than offset higher recurrent spending. Capital expenditure execution fell to a record low of 46.8 percent, reflecting implementation constraints, including disruptions following the September 2025 unrest, while recurrent spending increased due to the clearance of interest-subsidy arrears, higher civil-service allowances, and increased EXECUTIVE SUMMARY W O R L D B A N K G R O U P | 7 NEPAL DEVELOPMENT UPDATE | OCTOBER 2026 conditional grants. Public debt increased from 43.0 percent of GDP in FY25 to 45.1 percent in FY26, with external debt rising faster than domestic debt, partly due to the valuation effects of Nepalese rupee depreciation against the US dollar. Despite the increase in public debt, Nepal remains at a low risk of debt distress. AUGUST 2026 FLOOD AND ITS TRANSMISSION CHANNELS TO NEPAL’S ECONOMY On August 26, 2026, a glacially triggered mass movement in the Rasuwagadhi border region between Nepal and China rapidly transformed into an extreme flash flood and debris flow, causing widespread destruction. The resulting flood propagated through the BhoteKoshi and Trishuli river systems, causing extensive destruction across Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and Dhading districts. Satellite, drone, and field observations indicate exceptionally high sediment concentrations, severe riverbank erosion, channel widening, slope instability, and widespread sediment deposition along the river corridor. Although the flood wave progressively attenuated downstream, significant hydrological and geomorphic impacts extended for more than 150 km. The event also created significant secondary risks, including temporary landslide-dammed lakes, destabilized riverbanks, and persistent changes in river morphology, increasing the vulnerability of affected areas to subsequent landslides and flooding. The event followed a major glacially related flood in the same transboundary Himalayan corridor in July 2025, underscoring the repeated exposure of critical infrastructure and trade connectivity to such hazards.
The extensive downstream propagation of the flood cascade translated into severe human impacts across the affected corridor. According to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, as of September 26, 2026, 1,453 people had died, 5,285 people remained missing, while 13,795 people had been rescued.
The human toll was accompanied by substantial physical damage, economic losses, and recovery needs. The World Bank’s Global Rapid Post-Disaster Damage Estimation (GRADE) estimates total direct economic damage to physical assets at USD 1.66 billion, with infrastructure accounting for 83 percent, followed by residential buildings (11 percent) and non-residential buildings (6 percent), and impacts concentrated largely in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and Dhading districts. The Government’s preliminary Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment (RDNA) estimates total physical damage at USD1.81 billion, broadly consistent with the GRADE estimate, and total disaster effects, including losses from disruptions to productive activities, livelihoods, and essential services, at approximately USD 2.7 billion. Energy, including hydropower and the electricity grid, was the most affected infrastructure subsector, while economic activities and livelihoods accounted for the largest impacts within the productive sector. The preliminary RDNA estimates total recovery and reconstruction needs at approximately USD 4.8 billion, of which 98.8 percent is required for longer-term recovery and reconstruction, with infrastructure accounting for 65.5 percent of total needs.
The Government has introduced a package of fiscal, insurance, and financial sector measures to support affected households and businesses and facilitate recovery. Key measures include (a) customs duty waivers and adjustments for replacement of machinery, equipment, vehicles, and damaged imports; (b) tax relief and extended filing/payment deadlines; (c) faster insurance claims and advance payments of up to 50 percent; and (d) loan restructuring, repayment extensions, interest-rate relief, and financing for replacement of damaged assets. As part of the federal government’s measures, provincial and local governments have been requested to provide temporary concessions on property and business taxes, building approval fees, and other local charges for flood-damaged businesses and property.
The August 2026 flood is expected to affect Nepal’s economy through four primary transmission channels: energy, transportation, trade, and tourism. Agriculture and banking and insurance are also channels through which the economy would be affected, but with relatively lower potential impact. Energy, particularly hydropower, is the most critical transmission channel. The flood affected 12 hydropower projects, including 7 operational projects with a combined capacity of 256.1 MW and 5 projects under construction with a combined capacity of 395.02 MW, as well as a 25 MW solar facility. Damage to transmission infrastructure disrupted an additional 149.6 MW, bringing total affected generation and transmission capacity to approximately 430.7 MW, equivalent to 10.6 percent of Nepal’s FY26 installed hydropower and solar capacity. Transportation and trade are other key transmission channels, given the concentration of Nepal’s international and domestic trade along a limited number of corridors. More than 55 km of the 82-km Galchhi–Rasuwagadhi trade corridor was damaged, with 40 km completely washed away 8 along with 37 motorable bridges and 68 suspension bridges. The Rasuwagadhi crossing is the main port for Nepal-China bilateral trade, accounting for 2.2 percent of Nepal’s total merchandise imports, 10.8 percent of merchandise imports from China, and 47.3 percent of merchandise exports to China in FY26. Damage to the Prithvi Highway at Krishnabhir further compounded the disruption by affecting a critical artery connecting Kathmandu with southern Nepal and the Indian border, with implications for both international trade and domestic supply chains. To restore connectivity, the authorities have constructed a new track at Krishnabhir, and two-way traffic has resumed on September 17, 2026, but with considerable risk of additional closures due to heavy rainfall. However, this new track and other damaged sections along the corridor remain vulnerable for any potential geohazard and climate induced effects. Tourism is expected to face a potentially prolonged impact, reflecting both physical disruptions and heightened perceptions of travel risks. More than 200 hotels and restaurants were damaged across the affected districts, while access to major trekking and pilgrimage destinations—including Langtang, Gosaikunda, and the Kailash Mansarovar corridor—has been disrupted. The timing of the flood further compounds the impact, as the disruption occurred immediately before the main autumn tourism season (September–November), when tourist arrivals and trekking activity typically increase. The United Kingdom, Australia, Canada, and the United States subsequently updated their travel advisories for Nepal. OUTLOOK, RISKS, AND CHALLENGES The August 2026 flood is expected to have a material negative impact on Nepal’s economic prospects in the short term, with real GDP growth projected to slow to 3.7 percent in FY27, reflecting disruptions to industry and services. Industry is expected to be the main drag on growth, reflecting extensive damage to hydropower, solar energy, electricity transmission, and transport infrastructure, which will constrain electricity generation, production, and the movement of goods. Services are expected to be affected through disruptions to trade, transport, tourism, and financial activity, while agricultural losses are expected to have limited effects on aggregate output but significant impacts on livelihoods in affected areas. Reconstruction and rehabilitation activities are expected to begin supporting economic activity in FY27 and gain momentum in FY28, as damaged infrastructure and productive capacity are progressively restored, supporting a recovery in real GDP growth to 5.2 percent in FY28. The pace and strength of the recovery will depend on the speed and scale of reconstruction and restoration efforts.
Inflation is projected to remain broadly contained and within the Nepal Rastra Bank’s medium-term target of around 5 percent. However, localized crop losses and transport disruptions could generate price pressures in FY27, disproportionately affecting poorer households. Improved paddy production, easing global commodity prices, and moderating inflation in India could help contain headline inflation during FY27-28. The current account surplus is expected to narrow in FY27 and further in FY28, reflecting a wider merchandise trade deficit and weaker services exports in the near term, followed by a reconstruction-driven increase in import demand. In FY27, flood-related damage to hydropower and transmission infrastructure, including a loss of approximately 60 MW of export-oriented hydropower capacity, is expected to weigh on electricity exports, while heightened travel risks could reduce tourism receipts. These effects are expected to be partly offset by higher insurance service exports associated with claims received from foreign reinsurers and continued growth in IT exports. In FY28, reconstruction-related demand for construction materials, machinery, and equipment is expected to substantially increase imports, while hydropower and tourism exports could recover as damaged infrastructure is restored, additional generation capacity comes online, and international tourist arrivals rebound. Despite the narrowing of the current account surplus, foreign exchange reserves are expected to remain comfortably above the regulatory minimum for import coverage, supported by resilient remittance inflows and continued support from migrant workers, including their financial contributions to reconstruction efforts.
The fiscal deficit is projected to widen over the medium term, driven by higher relief and reconstruction spending and weaker revenue growth in the near term. In FY27, expenditure pressures are expected to increase as the government finances relief, initial reconstruction, and maintenance of public infrastructure damaged by the August 2026 flood, while revenue growth is constrained by tax relief measures, weaker import growth, and disruptions to economic activity. The deficit is expected to remain elevated in FY28 as reconstruction accelerates, although stronger revenue mobilization from reconstruction-related imports should gradually ease fiscal pressures. The deficit is expected to be financed through a mix of domestic and concessional external borrowing. Public debt is projected to increase from 45.1 percent of GDP in FY26 to 46.8 percent in FY27 and 47.9 percent in FY28, while Nepal is expected to remain at low risk of debt distress.
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY W O R L D B A N K G R O U P | 9 NEPAL DEVELOPMENT UPDATE | OCTOBER 2026 The risks to the outlook are tilted to the downside, with the pace and design of post-flood recovery representing a key domestic uncertainty. Prolonged conflict in the Middle East could reduce tourism and remittance inflows, weaken consumption and services activity, and dampen overall growth, while disruptions to fertilizer and fuel supplies could raise production costs and constrain agricultural output, investment, and broader economic activity. Domestically, delays in relief, reconstruction, and restoration of flood-damaged infrastructure could prolong disruptions to transport, trade, tourism, hydropower generation, and private sector activity, while the high share of uninsured assets could slow recovery and increase fiscal pressures. Financial sector vulnerabilities, including potential further deterioration in asset quality, could constrain private credit growth. On the upside, improved political stability and progress on structural reforms could strengthen investor confidence and support private investment and a faster recovery. BUILDING DIFFERENTLY AFTER THE AUGUST 2026 FLOOD: IMPLICATIONS FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND FUTURE INVESTMENT The August 26, 2026, flood highlighted the scale and complexity of disaster risk in Nepal’s Himalayan environment, demonstrating how a single extreme event can generate cascading impacts across communities, transport networks, energy infrastructure, livelihoods, and essential services. Recovery should therefore go beyond restoring damaged assets to reconsider how future development in highly exposed mountain environments can better account for changing and interconnected risks as well as avoiding the accumulation of risk in a concentrated area. Reconstruction planning should be informed by updated multi-hazard risk assessments that consider floods, debris flows, landslides, glacial hazards, and river-system dynamics, as well as the potential for cascading impacts across entire infrastructure networks. This includes greater attention to the location and design of critical infrastructure and to lifeline systems— transport, energy, communications, and other networks essential to maintaining connectivity and basic services. Building redundancy and alternative connections into critical networks can also reduce the consequences of failure of individual roads, bridges, transmission lines, or other key assets.
Strengthening risk information, regional and project specific monitoring and early warning, and preparedness should complement physical reconstruction. The event underscores the importance of improved hydrometeorological and high-altitude monitoring, faster communication of risk information, and stronger early warning systems that reach exposed communities and institutions. Given the transboundary nature of Himalayan hazards and river systems, stronger mechanisms for upstream information exchange and cross-border data sharing should also be considered. Recovery should additionally address livelihoods, local economic activity, tourism, trade, and access to essential services alongside physical assets. This requires effective coordination across levels of government and sectors at the regional and local level, disaster risk financing, mechanisms for rapid access to resources, and preparedness to manage large and complex recovery operations. Nepal’s development of an Integrated Social Protection System (ISPS), with an integrated social registry as a core building block, could provide an important foundation for identifying vulnerable households and rapidly scaling disaster assistance through appropriate payment arrangements.
The recovery provides an opportunity to move from “Build Back Better” towards “Build Differently.” In some locations, rebuilding the same infrastructure in the same place—even to a higher engineering standard—may not adequately address the underlying risk. Future investment decisions could instead incorporate updated hazard information, more careful consideration of location, accumulation of risk, and design, greater redundancy in critical networks, and stronger monitoring and early warning at the regional and local levels. The objective is not necessarily to create new institutions or frameworks, but to identify where existing arrangements worked well, where gaps became apparent, and where targeted improvements can strengthen resilience. In this way, reconstruction can support not only recovery from the August 2026 flood but also a more resilient development pathway for Nepal’s Himalayas. The goal is to build resilient systems that continue functioning when individual assets fail and reduce the impact of future disasters.

Services sector The services sector grew by 4.2 percent in FY26, slightly lower than the 4.4 percent in FY25, reflecting mixed performance across its subcomponents (Figure 5). Financial and insurance activities recorded the strongest growth, reaching 9.2 percent in FY26, up from 7.5 percent in FY25. This was driven by premiums growth of 12.3 percent and 15.6 percent for life insurance and non-life insurance sectors, respectively (see Financial Sector section). Growth in non-life insurance sector premium was particularly strong despite a modest 6.9 percent increase in the number of policies issued in FY26. This may reflect increased demand for insurance coverage, especially from higher-premium lines such as property insurance and engineering and contractor liability coverage, following the September 2025 unrest, when large businesses experienced significant damage. Similarly, wholesale and retail trade grew by 4.5 percent in FY26, from 3.9 percent in FY25, supported by higher merchandise imports and strong private consumption underpinned by large remittance inflows.

Gross Domestic Product by Demand Private consumption was a key driver of economic growth in FY26, boosted by high remittance inflows. Remittance inflows reached 35.8 percent of GDP in FY26, supporting 14 food inflation, which dropped by 3.7 percentage points to 1.0 percent in FY26 (Figure 7). The slowdown in food inflation was broad-based, with cereal grains, pulses and legumes, and vegetables recording the largest prices declines. Increased supply from domestic and international markets, including continued imports from India, alongside weak domestic demand contributed to the lower prices across these food categories. Meanwhile, prices of meat and fish, ghee and edible oil, and fruits increased in FY26, with the largest increases recorded for ghee and oil and fruits. Higher domestic fuel prices and transportation costs, increased input costs amid global supply chain disruptions associated with the Middle East conflict, and the nominal depreciation of the Nepali rupee against the US dollar contributed to the increase in the prices of ghee and oil. A bird flu outbreak contributed to the rise in the prices of meat and eggs in FY26. The increase in fruit prices was driven by import restrictions on key fruits, including bananas from India, due to disease concerns, lower domestic production amid erratic weather conditions, and higher transport and fuel costs.
Non-food and services inflation rose by 0.5 percentage points to 4.2 percent in FY26, driven by higher prices of transport and miscellaneous goods and services. The increase in transport prices reflected higher domestic fuel prices and higher prices for road and air transportation amid elevated international oil prices associated with the conflict in the Middle East. Higher prices of miscellaneous goods and services partly reflected higher domestic prices of gold and silver, driven by higher global prices.

Exports of goods and services also contributed to economic growth in FY26 but at a slower pace. Growth in electricity exports, supported by higher hydropower generation and increased cross-border electricity trade, contributed to overall export growth. This was partly offset by a significantly lower growth in the value of exports of edible oils in FY26 compared with the exceptionally high growth recorded in FY25, reflecting a base effect. In FY25, exports of edible oils increased sharply after India raised import duties on refined and crude edible oil in late 2024 and mid-2025, creating greater arbitrage opportunities for Nepali exporters that benefited from zero-tariff access to India under the SAFTA agreement.
Investment’s contribution to economic growth was limited by a contraction of public investment in FY26. Public investment declined, reflecting weaker capital budget execution in FY26, which reached a six-year low (see Fiscal Sector section). This reflected structural delays and disruptions related to the political transition following the September 2025 unrest. Moreover, non-hydropower private investment was also affected in FY26, as investors adopted a wait-and- see approach due to heightened uncertainties amidst political transition.

However, this inflation differential is largely related to non-India major trade partners. In contrast, inflation in both India and Nepal has been declining since FY24, resulting in a narrowing of the inflation differential between the two countries. This convergence in the inflation rate reflects (a) higher trade integration, with India accounting for about 60 percent of Nepal’s total merchandise international trade, (b) extensive cross-border labor mobility which supports a convergence in wage growth between the two countries, and (c) the transmission of India’s inflation shocks directly to Nepal. 18 RECENT ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENTS A.3 MONETARY AND FINANCIAL SECTOR The Nepal Rastra Bank reduced the policy rate and narrowed the interest rate corridor in FY26 The Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB) maintained a cautiously accommodative monetary policy stance for the third consecutive year in FY26. In FY26, the central bank reduced the policy rate twice-by 50 basis points (bps) in July 2025 and 25 bps in December 2025-lowering it to 4.25 percent, from 5.0 percent in FY25 (Figure 16). To strengthen monetary policy transmission, the NRB also lowered the upper and lower bounds of the interest rate corridor by 75 bps and 25 bps to 5.75 percent and 2.75 percent, respectively, effectively narrowing the gap between the floor and the ceiling.
Declining policy rates alongside persistent excess liquidity drove down money market rates. The weighted average interbank rate of banks and financial institutions— the operating target of monetary policy fell by 0.25 bps in FY26, remaining close to the lower bound of the interest rate corridor. Excess liquidity, alongside the reduction in policy rates, contributed to lower deposit and lending interest rates. Amid sluggish credit demand and excess liquidity, the average nominal deposit interest rate dropped by 122 bps y/y, while the average nominal lending interest rate fell by 161 bps y/y in FY26, reaching historic lows of 3.6 and 7.1 percent, respectively (Figure 18). Existing regulatory guidelines permit banks and financial institutions to modify deposit and lending rates monthly, provided adjustments remain within prescribed limits.

NRB Regulatory and Forbearance Measures in FY26 The NRB introduced targeted regulatory measures in FY26 to cushion the impact of various shocks on asset quality, strengthen capital buffers, and safeguard financial stability. The measures included one-time loan rescheduling and restructuring facilities for businesses and borrowers affected by natural disasters, social unrest, and disruptions at key customs points, as well as for selected construction and real estate companies. The August 2026 flood occurred in a transboundary Himalayan corridor that had already experienced a major glacially related flood one year earlier. On July 8, 2025, a glacial flood originating upstream in China affected the Rasuwagadhi border area of Rasuwa, causing extensive damage to settlements, transport infrastructure, hydropower facilities, and the Nepal–China border crossing. A.5 AUGUST 2026 RASUWA FLOOD On August 26, 2026, a catastrophic glacially triggered mass movement occurred in the Rasuwagadhi border region between Nepal and China7. The failure mobilized a large volume of ice, rock, water, and sediment from elevations above 5,000 m and rapidly evolved into an extreme flash flood and debris flow. The glacial collapse was of such a scale that a seismic signal equivalent to a M5.2 earthquake was generated. The resulting flood traveled downstream through the BhoteKoshi and Trishuli river systems, causing severe destruction across Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and Dhading districts (Figure 33).

Satellite, drone, and field observations indicate that the initial mass movement descended through the upper catchment before entering the Chusumdo Tsangpo valley, where extensive deposition and rapid transformation into a water-rich, sediment-laden flood occurred. By approximately 10-15 km downstream from the source area, the event exhibited the characteristics of a major flash flood carrying exceptionally high sediment concentrations. The flood maintained extreme flow depths and velocities over long distances. Substantial riverbank erosion, channel widening, slope undercutting, and widespread sediment deposition were observed along the Trishuli River corridor. Although the flood wave attenuated progressively downstream, elevated water levels and geomorphic impacts were evident over more than 150 km of river corridor. Peak impacts occurred in the upper and middle reaches, while flood effects diminished substantially farther downstream toward Bharatpur. The disaster also generated significant secondary risks. These included the formation of temporary landslide-dammed lakes, increased landslide susceptibility along destabilized riverbanks, and major changes to river morphology caused by extensive sediment deposition. The extensive downstream propagation of the flood cascade translated into severe human impacts across the affected corridor. According to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA), as of September 26, 2026, 1,453 people had died, 5,285 people remained missing, while 13,795 people had been rescued8. The geographic distribution of casualties and missing persons indicates that the human impacts extended well beyond the immediate source area and followed the downstream footprint of the flood cascade.
The human toll was accompanied by substantial physical damage and economic impacts. According to the World Bank’s Global Rapid Post-Disaster Damage Estimation (GRADE) report, total direct economic damage to physical assets was 8 https://ndrrma.gov.np/np/situation-report/450 26 RECENT ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENTS estimated at USD 1.66 billion. Infrastructure accounted for the largest share of damage, at USD 1.38 billion (83 percent), followed by residential buildings at USD 185 million (11 percent) and non-residential buildings at USD 101 million (6 percent). Damage was relatively localized, with the vast majority of physical impacts concentrated in three districts: Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and Dhading. Rasuwa was the most affected district, accounting for USD 1.07 billion (64 percent) of total direct damage, followed by Nuwakot with an estimated USD 551 million and Dhading with approximately USD 39 million. The Government’s preliminary Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment (RDNA)9 reports a broadly comparable level of physical damage, while capturing a wider range of economic impacts when losses are considered. The RDNA estimates total physical damage at USD 1.81 billion, broadly consistent with the GRADE estimate of USD 1.66 billion. The RDNA additionally estimates USD 883.32 million in losses, bringing total disaster effects to approximately USD 2.7 billion. This broader estimate captures not only the destruction of physical assets but also the economic losses associated with disruptions to productive activities, livelihoods, and essential services. The infrastructure sector accounts for 46.5 percent of total disaster effects, followed by the productive sector at 36.8 percent and the social sector at 16.6 percent. Within the infrastructure sector, energy—including hydropower and the electricity grid—is the most severely affected subsector, with total disaster effects estimated at USD 997.1 million. Within the productive sector, economic activities and livelihoods represent the largest impact, with total effects estimated at USD 965.1 million. The scale of these impacts translates into substantial recovery and reconstruction requirements. The RDNA estimates total recovery needs at approximately USD 4.8 billion, equivalent to around 1.8 times the assessed damage and losses. Of the total recovery requirement, USD 58 million (1.2 percent) is identified for short-term recovery during the first six months, while approximately USD 4.7 billion (98.8 percent) is identified for longer-term recovery and reconstruction. Infrastructure accounts for approximately 65.5 percent of total recovery needs, followed by the social sector at 14.3 percent, the productive sector (agriculture, fisheries, livestock, banking, and economic activities) at 7.0 percent, and cross-cutting needs at 7.2 percent. 5.1 GOVERNMENT’S ANNOUNCED MEASURES IN THE AFTERMATH OF THE AUGUST 2026 FLOOD The government has introduced a package of fiscal, insurance, and financial sector measures to support flood-affected households and businesses and facilitate the recovery of productive capacity (Annex 1). Key elements of package support measures include: (a) customs duty waivers and adjustments for replacement machinery, equipment, vehicles, and damaged imports; (b) tax relief and extended filing/payment deadlines for affected taxpayers; (c) faster insurance claim processing and advance payments of up to 50 percent; and (d) loan restructuring, repayment extensions, interest-rate relief, and financing for replacement of damaged assets through banks and financial institutions. As part of the federal government’s measures, provincial and local governments have been requested to provide temporary concessions on property and business taxes, building approval fees, and other local charges related to flood-damaged businesses and property. 5.2 TRANSMISSION CHANNELS OF AUGUST 2026 FLOOD ON NEPAL’S ECONOMY The August 2026 flood is expected to affect Nepal’s economy through four primary transmission channels: energy, transportation, trade, and tourism. Agriculture and banking and insurance are also channels through which the economy would be affected, although with relatively lower potential impact.
