3 Client Capability and PIU Assessment 3.1 Experience Recent projects such as the IDA funded IFRDP have helped to create a small team of professionals within ANE who have gained significant experience of delivering infrastructure under World Bank funding and conditions. A dedicated Project Implementation Unit (PIU) has been established within ANE which will focus exclusively on the World Bank projects that impact on the road sector. This PIU currently covers the IFRDP, the SATCP and the MPA (SRSEIP). The staff allocated to this PIU are recognised as being some of the most experienced employed by ANE. A similar PIU will be established in the MTC which will provide similar implementation management for the relevant activities.
The major works under the MPA are to be implemented following the Output and Performance-Based Road Contract (OPBRC) approach. In recent years, ANE has managed OPBRC works in the province of Gaza. These works were initiated in response to climate emergencies and were also financed by WB. Four sections of road were rehabilitated following extensive damage from flooding. A concept design was prepared and four civil works contracts were then tendered for repair and rehabilitation works on sections of the N220, N221, R859 and the R452. These contracts omitted the longer-term maintenance normally expected with OPBRC projects as they included 23 Design and Build only. Initial difficulties were encountered due to the lack of familiarity with OPBRC contract forms. This shortcoming extended to the consultants and the contractors who also exhibited an initial lack of understanding of the expectations of OPBRC largely due to the lack of experience. Despite some delays, these works were successfully implemented. The learning curve has now been traversed and the road sector actors at the appropriate level are now generally aware of the particularities of OPBRC. ANE has an ongoing OPBRC contract under the IFRDP that covers the rehabilitation and improvement of the N10/N1 from Quelimane to Namacurra (68km).
Hence, the combined experience now available within ANE and the pool of service providers is sufficient to raise the expectation that successful implementation of performance-based road infrastructure contracts is achievable. Despite this, ANE intends to include the recruitment of an experienced Procurement Specialist and two procurement officers to reinforce the PIU for an initial period of two years with the objective of reducing the workload on the existing staff which will help to reduce delays in processing procurement issues. Funding for these positions will come from the IFRDP budget. MTC also plan to recruit a procurement specialist to help support their procurement activities. In this case, funding will be made available under Component 3 of the MPA.

8 Summary of PPSD to inform the Bank’s preparation of the PAD 8.1 Recommended Procurement Approach for the Project a. Contract Strategy Goods, services and civil works will be prepared in economical packages to attract local and foreign bidders who are qualified, can offer good prices 33 and can demonstrate their ability to complete contracts within stipulated timeframe resulting in good value for money.
Packaging for procurement is decided in such a way that encourages adequate participation and is based on two principal forms of procurement packaging. (i) the grouping (or bulking) of procurement requirements within a procurement category for the purpose of acquiring them under a single contract, and (ii) the division of one requirement into multiple lots, where bidders can submit bids for one, several or all lots (as would be stipulated in the procurement documents), and where a contract could be awarded for each lot.
The following have been taken into account when considering procurement packaging: i.
The likelihood of local suppliers being able to fulfill the requirements and whether the packaging would limit their participation.
ii.
If the group of requirements are needed (or can be received) simultaneously or whether there are different delivery dates between requirements. Unless the selected supplier can deliver at the various selected delivery intervals, receiving all the goods at one time could result in a potential logistical problem; therefore, under these circumstances it may be preferable not to package the various requirements.
iii.
The availability of several suppliers that can provide a combination of procurement categories as may be required in the case of supply, installation, commissioning and training.
iv.
If the PIU lacks the capacity to coordinate several suppliers, this may create a preference for packaging to reduce the number of suppliers that the PIU would have to coordinate.

results.title: Thailand cabinet approves $313 million flood relief, official says | Reuters
results.content:
BANGKOK, Oct 20 (Reuters) - Thailand's cabinet has approved 10.5 billion baht ($312.7 ​million) in flood relief, alongside other ‌measures including debt-payment suspensions and soft loans, government officials said on Tuesday. [...] The government had ​previously paid more than 5 ​billion baht in flood assistance, government ⁠spokesperson Ekkapob Pianpises told a ​briefing
 The cabinet also approved tax relief ​and customs duty exemptions for flood victims, a finance ministry official said
 In September, Bangkok ​was declared a disaster-affected zone after nearly ​300 mm (12 inches) of rain hit the ‌city ⁠in just three days, as much as it typically receives in the whole of the month
 Bank of Thailand Deputy Governor ​Piti Disyatat told Reuters last ​week ⁠the floods would not significantly affect the economy, which is expected to grow ⁠2.3% ​or higher this year

BLUEPRINT 2.0 Geospatial Landscape of the United Nations system The picture shows the Secretary-General opening the 78th General Assembly Debate.
Credits: UN Photo Library The direction set out in the Blueprint 2.0 places greater emphasis on the foundations that make this work possible. This includes strengthening data systems, improving standards, and investing in capacity at country and regional levels. It also recognizes the importance of partnerships and the responsible use of emerging technologies, including geospatial artiﬁcial intelligence, to expand what is possible while ensuring that these tools are used in ways that are inclusive and accountable.
This Landscape offers a system-wide view of current geospatial activities, resources and capacities. By bringing these together, it aims to support stronger collaboration, reduce fragmentation and make it easier to learn from one another. It also provides a basis for identifying where further investment and coordination are needed.
As the United Nations system continues to evolve, geospatial information will remain a critical part of how it delivers on its mandates. Strengthening its use is not only about better data. It is about making better decisions, responding more effectively and supporting Member States in navigating an increasingly complex world.
Dejan Jakovljevic CIO and Director, Digitalization and Informatics Division , Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) We are living in a time of growing complexity. Climate pressures are intensifying, health systems continue to face new demands, and inequalities remain deeply embedded across societies. At the same time, advances in data and technology are changing how decisions are made. In this context, understanding place, location and connection has become more important than ever. Geospatial information is no longer a technical add-on. It is central to how the United Nations system understands the world and responds to it.
Across the United Nations, geospatial approaches are becoming part of everyday practice. They are used to identify where needs are greatest, to support planning and delivery, and to monitor progress over time. Whether in humanitarian response, public health, environmental monitoring or development programming, geospatial information helps ensure that action is grounded in real-world conditions and reaches the people and places most at risk.
The United Nations Geospatial Network has played an important role in bringing greater coherence to this work. By strengthening coordination and encouraging shared approaches, the Network supports a more connected geospatial ecosystem across entities. This updated Geospatial Landscape of the United Nations System reﬂects that progress. It shows how geospatial capabilities are being used across mandates and highlights the growing links between geospatial, statistical and other data systems.

Credits: UN Photo/Rick Bajornas (2017) “The Secretariat, one of the main organs of the UN, is organized along departmental lines, with each department or ofﬁce having a distinct area of action and responsibility. Ofﬁces and departments coordinate with each other to ensure cohesion as they carry out the day-to-day work of the Organization in ofﬁces and duty stations around the world. At the head of the United Nations Secretariat is the Secretary-General.
” SECRETARIAT 2 BLUEPRINT 2.0 GEOSPATIAL LANDSCAPE OF THE UNITED NATIONS SYSTEM Department of Economic and Social Affairs (DESA) Geospatial Activities The United Nations Statistics Division (UNSD), one of the ten constituent entities of the Department of Economic and Social Affairs (DESA), serves as the central body for statistical and geospatial activities within the United Nations. UNSD has Secretariat responsibility of three intergovernmental, subsidiary bodies of the United Nations Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC):  The United Nations Statistical Commission;  The United Nations Committee of Experts on Global Geospatial Information Management (UN-GGIM); and  The United Nations Group of Experts on Geographical Names (UNGEGN).
The Statistical Commission is the apex entity of the global statistical system. It is the highest decision-making body for international statistical activities, including the setting of statistical standards and norms, measuring progress on the implementation of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), the development of concepts and methods and supporting implementation at national and international levels.
UN-GGIM is the leading intergovernmental mechanism for making joint decisions and setting directions on the production, availability and use of geospatial information within national, regional and global policy frameworks. It also develops strategies to strengthen geospatial information capacity, especially in developing countries. UN-GGIM helps countries access accurate data and build integrated, interoperable and accessible information systems to support development.
UNGEGN encourages the standardization of geographical names and promotes the national and international beneﬁts of standardization.
UNSD also provides substantive guidance and supervision of the Global Centres of Excellence, as ofﬁces away from Headquarters:  The United Nations Global Geodetic Centre of Excellence (UN-GGCE), based at the United Nations Campus in Bonn (Germany), envisions a world where all countries are supported in geodesy to accelerate SDGs progress and realise social, environmental and economic beneﬁts. Its main objective is to implement General Assembly resolution 69/266 by working with Member States and geodetic organizations to strengthen collective impact, enhance investment in the global geodesy supply chain, expand technical assistance and raise awareness of geodesy and its beneﬁts.  The United Nations Global Geospatial Knowledge and Innovation (UN-GGKIC), based in Deqing (People’s Republic of China), aims to advance implementation of the United Nations Integrated Geospatial Information Framework (UN-IGIF), strengthen geospatial management capacity in Member States and to promote knowledge sharing and innovation.  The United Nations Global Geospatial Ecosystem Centre of Excellence is being established in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.
Geospatial Data Geospatial data collation and dissemination activities are available on the UNSD website:  The World Geographical Names Database, managed by UNGEGN, provides standardized geographical names.  Automatic Identiﬁcation System (AIS) data powers the IMF’s PortWatch platform, which monitors and simulates maritime trade disruptions to support decision-making on future trade shocks.  The United Nations Comtrade database aggregates trade statistics from approximately 200 countries, representing over 99 per cent of the global merchandise trade. 1designated Secretariat offce to the Secretariat to the Committee of Experts on Global Geospatial Information Management pursuant to Resolution E/2011/24 and as Secretariat to the Network E/C.20/2018/18/Add.1.
3 SECRETARIAT Geospatial Usage As the Secretariat for UN-GGIM, UNSD provides a forum for Member States to make joint decisions and set direction regarding the production, availability and application of geospatial information within national, regional and global policy frameworks. This work helps address global challenges regarding the use of geospatial information, including in the development agendas, such as the 2030 Agenda. 4 BLUEPRINT 2.0 GEOSPATIAL LANDSCAPE OF THE UNITED NATIONS SYSTEM Offce of Information and Communications Technology (OICT) Geospatial Activities The vision of geospatial services in the United Nations Secretariat is centred on effective, efﬁcient and universal use of geospatial information to support all mandates and operations of the United Nations for a better world, as outlined in the United Nations Geospatial Strategy. The Geospatial Information Section, in collaboration with United Nations Global Service Centre (UNGSC)[1] and ﬁeld operations, leads efforts to mainstream the use of geospatial information across the Secretariat, ensuring integrated and accessible information, analysis and visualisation for evidence-based decision-making in support of peace and security, human rights, international law, sustainable development and humanitarian aid.
The mission to mainstream geospatial information and innovation in support of the United Nations mandates is pursued through the following four primary goals:  Provide universal fundamental global geospatial data, standards, methods, tools and services  Enhance geospatial information beneﬁts for mandate, operational and decision-making requirements  Increase capacity, expertise and integrated geospatial systems across the Organization  Raise awareness on geospatial information and harness international partnerships Activities include: 1. Oversight of geospatial strategies and policies for the Secretariat, including the responsibilities on “Guidelines for the Publication of Maps” as per ST/AI 189/Add.25/ Rev.1.
2. Serving as co-Secretariat to the United Nations Committee of Experts on Global Geospatial Information Management (UN-GGIM) with the DESA Statistics Division. 3. Providing cartographic and geospatial services to the Security Council, senior management, Secretariat ofﬁces and ﬁeld operations. 4. Preparing and disseminating ofﬁcial United Nations cartographic products, including web-map services under the United Nations imprint, as set forth in administrative instruction (ST/AI/189/Add.25/Rev.1) to ensure conformity with publication standards. 5. Maintaining and distributing global geospatial datasets, from Member States to the Secretariat and its agencies, funds and programmes, including managing the Second Administrative Level Boundaries (SALB) programme, which provides validated authoritative administrative units’ data. 6. Providing technical assistance on international boundary demarcation processes referred to the Secretary-General by Member States, for peacebuilding and conﬂict prevention. 7 . Coordinating with the Client Service Delivery section (CSDS) at UNGSC to support geospatial ﬁeld operations.
8. Coordinating inter-agency efforts on cooperation, capacity building and innovation, including United Nations open geographic information system (GIS) and GeoAI.
9. As part of its broader responsibilities, the geospatial services at the UNGSC are key to providing standardized and centralized support to the Secretariat and its ﬁeld operations.
Geospatial Data and Technology Geospatial services include base and thematic maps and access to global datasets on geography, common and military operational data, populated places and Member States’ shared topographic mapping data (MGCP1). Subnational unit data, published in liaison with national authorities through the SALB programme. This supports common geographies that facilitate disaggregation and aggregation in spatial analysis for the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). To centralize online storage and streamline data dissemination, digital platforms such as websites, United Nations Geohub and United Nations Geoportal have been deployed and maintained. These platforms provide easy access to fundamental datasets, standardized cartography and web-map/feature services. In addition, a wide range of satellite imagery analysis and interpretation products are produced for the Security Council, United Nations Secretariat departments and ofﬁces, United Nations ﬁeld missions and upon request, 5 SECRETARIAT to United Nations agencies, funds and programmes. The Global Service Centre conducts research and pilots geospatial applications and tools in emerging areas such as virtual reality (VR), digital twins and the incorporation of open-source data and technology.
Geospatial Usage Geospatial support services encompass data management, image processing, interpretation, analysis, mapping support and advanced analytics. These services underpin the Situational Awareness platforms, including geospatial visualisation to enhance operational understanding, geospatial analysis to support decision-making and the development of smart knowledge-based platforms for mission operations. Geospatial data supports a wide range of cartographic outputs, analytics and applications, many of which are integrated into enterprise or decision-support systems. These capabilities underpin corporate web services on ofﬁcial United Nations platforms and beneﬁt both Headquarters and ﬁeld missions. The core software infrastructure is based on Esri technologies, with growing integration of open-source solutions to support a hybrid systems architecture. Artiﬁcial intelligence and machine learning further enhance productivity in data management, image analysis and interpretation.
Geospatial information supports the fulﬁlment of core United Nations mandates, such as remote monitoring of ceaseﬁre agreements and armed group activities, protection of civilians and the provision of electoral assistance. In emergency and crisis situations, geospatial data are critical for identifying the locations of vulnerable populations, supporting search and rescue operations, mapping mineﬁelds and other restricted areas and supporting evacuation planning and crisis response. Geospatial Resources At the United Nations Headquarters in New York (USA), the geospatial team comprises nine staff: one Section Chief, four Geospatial Information Ofﬁcers, one Geospatial Assistant, one support staff member and two UNOPS Geospatial Information Ofﬁcers. An additional forty geospatial support staff members are also based at these locations. Across peace operations and special political missions4 approximately 100 geospatial personnel are deployed. This includes ofﬁcers, ﬁeld and national staff and military geospatial ofﬁcers provided through troop contribution by Member States. OLA/DOALOS, supported by relevant General Assembly resolutions5, established a Geographic Information Management (GIM) cluster to fulﬁl its responsibilities involving the management, analysis and dissemination of geospatial information under UNCLOS. The GIM cluster work programme includes:  Maintenance of a geospatial information database for the custody of charts and lists of geographical coordinates submitted by States under UNCLOS, in relation to the limits of maritime zones, including lines of delimitation.  Provision of geospatial services to the Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf (CLCS), as part of providing Secretariat services for CLCS consideration of complex geological, geomorphological, geophysical and hydrographical data contained in the submissions of coastal States, in accordance with article 76 of UNCLOS.  Development and maintenance of a geoportal on maritime limits and boundaries, intended to give due publicity, via the Internet, to information deposited or otherwise provided by States.  Assistance to the International Hydrographic Organization (IHO), as appropriate, with the initial implementation, testing and evaluation of product speciﬁcations for the structure of the deposited information, to ensure its compatibility with geographic information systems, electronic nautical charts and other systems.  Provision of geospatial information management and analysis to the bodies and/or States to which the Secretary-General provides support for peaceful settlement of disputes, and other parts of the United Nations system engaged in maritime boundary delimitation processes.  Provision of cartographic brieﬁng materials on law of the sea and ocean affairs-related matters, upon request by the ofﬁces of the Secretary-General, the Deputy Secretary-General, the United Nations Legal Counsel, the Assistant Secretary-General for Legal Affairs and/ or the Ofﬁce of the Spokesperson for the Secretary-General. Geospatial Data and Technology The GIM cluster maintains a geospatial database with the outer limits of maritime zones, including lines of delimitation, based on lists of geographical coordinates and nautical charts submitted by States. The database is built on product speciﬁcations developed in cooperation with the International Hydrographic Organization (IHO).
The cluster also manages geological, geomorphological, geophysical and hydrographical data submitted by coastal States to the CLCS. This data are augmented by lines of delimitation contained in maritime boundary delimitation treaties registered with the Secretariat in accordance with article 102 of the Charter of the United Nations, and by the outer limits of maritime zones, including lines of delimitation, which have otherwise been communicated by States to the Secretary-General. UNDRR supports countries in the implementation, monitoring and sharing of risk reduction strategies to minimize existing risk and prevent the creation of new risk. Geospatial information is key to the implementation of the Sendai Framework, as recognized by the United Nations General Assembly in 2019 in its resolution on Disaster Risk Reduction, which included a paragraph which “ … recognizes the endorsement by the Economic and Social Council on 2 July 2018 of the Strategic Framework on Geospatial Information and Services for Disasters, as a guide for Member States to ensure the availability and accessibility of quality geospatial information and services across all phases of disaster risk reduction and management, and which contributes to the implementation of the Sendai Framework” . UNDRR is strengthening disaster loss accounting globally to support country assessments of hazard risk, and also to ensure that countries have in place a comprehensive and credible accounting system for recording and reporting disaster events. This builds on the support UNDRR has been providing to Member States for over 20 years in the implementation of national disaster loss accounting systems. Such systems support countries’ assessment of risk, provide essential information for the development of DRR strategies and investment decisions at the local and national levels, as well as facilitate the reporting on progress in the implementation of the Sendai Framework by ensuring countries have compiled the disaster loss data needed to report through the Sendai Framework Monitor, which countries use to report progress against the agreed global targets and indicators.
The “SFM Analytics” module of the online Sendai Framework Monitoring system gives open access to multiple forms of analysis of Member States’ validated data. Furthermore, as per the United Nations Statistical Commission’s recommendation, UNDRR is working with the United Nations Statistics Division and United Nations Regional Commissions on a global framework for disaster-related statistics that will help National Statistics Organizations make this an integral part of ofﬁcial statistics. In addition, and in order to further support countries in developing and improving their disaster risk assessments, UNDRR is providing a secretariat function to the Global Risk Assessment Framework (GRAF), launched in 2019. In its next phase of operationalization, GRAF will pilot systemic risk assessment in various country contexts. One of the important data sources being considered in assessing systemic risk is geospatial and Earth observation data, and discussions are ongoing with both UN-GGIM and the Group on Earth Observations (GEO) Secretariat to forge a strong partnership for the initiative. UNDRR is currently developing the United Nations Global Assessment Report 2022 (GAR 2022), in close collaboration with UN-GGIM and the GEO Secretariat. Geospatial and Earth observation data will complement Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) statistical data provided by UN DESA and data coming out of the UNDRR managed Sendai Framework Monitor, to assess trends in disaster risk and losses, but also to identify synergies, interlinkages and trade-offs in simultaneously reaching the global goals and the Sendai Framework targets. With the support of geospatial and Earth observation data, GAR 2022 will also assess the positive impacts that risk reduction has had on other major global agendas Geospatial Data and Technology UNDRR supports Member States in the development of disaster loss databases and is custodian of the disaster loss data reported through the Sendai Framework Monitor. These data can be accessed publicly through the Analytics Module of the Sendai Framework Monitor. 15 SECRETARIAT Geospatial Resources UNDRR provides direct support to Member States through its ﬁve regional ofﬁces in areas which include the development and maintenance of disaster loss databases, monitoring progress in the implementation of the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction and the development of national and local risk reduction assessments.

The mandate of UNODC covers thematic areas related to preventing and countering transnational organized crime, corruption, terrorism and the world drug problem, along with strengthening criminal justice systems. The Research and Trend Analysis Branch (RAB) of UNODC produces a variety of studies on drugs and crime (e.g., prevalence of drug use, corruption, homicide rates and ﬁrearm seizures), all of which incorporate geospatial data and analytics at varying levels and scales. One of the heaviest users of geospatial data and processing is the Illicit Crop Monitoring Programme (ICMP), which has generated statistics on illicit crop cultivation and production of cocaine, opium and cannabis since the early 2000s. Since 2016, RAB has also employed Earth observation (EO) technologies to monitor other crimes, including illegal mining and deforestation.
RAB participates in various partnership projects that leverage geospatial data and open-source intelligence, including for detecting illicit activities using EO data and technologies. It also supports capacity-building for the use of geospatial data in monitoring mining activities and assessing their environmental impact.
These activities are supported by funding from Member States, the European Space Agency and the United Nations Development Account, which enable both research and capacity-building in the use of EO technology and geospatial analytics. UNODC also works with a global network of research institutions and academic partners to develop methodologies and tools.
RAB is additionally engaged in innovation projects, including GeoAI initiatives with the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) focused on detecting illegal airstrips and the automated generation of agricultural maps.
Geospatial Data and Technology Each year, UNODC acquires a large volume of very-high-resolution (VHR) imagery from commercial vendors, and high-resolution (HR) imagery through programmes such as Norway’s International Climate and Forests Initiative (NICFI). Medium-resolution imagery, such as Landsat and Sentinel, is accessed via open platforms. Ground-truth data are collected using global positioning systems (GPS), alongside geo-tagged photos and videos gathered during ﬁeld visits and aerial overﬂights with planes, helicopters or drones. Field-level geospatial data on illicit crop cultivation are derived from satellite imagery and complemented by auxiliary data, typically secondary geospatial data sourced online or from partner agencies, to inform models for sampling frames, potential agriculture zones and risk mapping. Thematic maps and other visualisations are embedded into UNODC reports and publications. UNODC provides interactive access to geospatial data, with spatial data products shared through online services and platforms:  Web-map publication and services using PowerBI and ArcGIS Online  Drugs Monitoring Platform, where government agencies submit location-based drug seizure reports, which are visualised on a web interface. These data are supplemented by additional seizure information extracted from media sources using web-scraping tools. Geospatial Usage The Illicit Crop Monitoring Programme (ICMP) processes over a thousand satellite images annually to estimate areas under illicit crop cultivation and to monitor other criminal activities, such as illegal mining. It produces maps and statistical graphics illustrating the distribution and evolution of cultivated ﬁelds, alongside related themes such as land use and socioeconomic indicators. Satellite imagery is analysed at various spatial (very-high, high, medium, low) and spectral resolutions (e.g., visible light, near-infrared). Very-high- and high-resolution imagery (e.g., Pleiades, WorldView) are primarily used to delineate crop ﬁelds, while medium- to low-resolution imagery (e.g., 17 SECRETARIAT Landsat, Sentinel) supports the development of sampling frames, land cover and risk maps and crop phenology analysis. Ground-truth data are collected in the ﬁeld to support validation and quality control. ICMP data are primarily analysed in ﬁeld ofﬁces, where interpretation, analysis and visualisation are conducted. At headquarters, RAB ensures quality control, assurance and coordination of geospatial projects. Findings are published in annual survey reports, which include methodologies sections and numerous maps.
UNODC also conducts geospatial research related to crime and drug issues, including corruption, drug use, trafﬁcking of ﬁrearms and fuel. Flagship publications such as the World Drug Report and the Global Study on Homicide feature numerous static and dynamic maps. The Smuggling of Migrants Observatory employs story maps to communicate key trends and research ﬁndings. The Drugs Monitoring Platform (DMP) maintains a global database of exact drug-seizure locations and offers a dedicated web-map service to visualise those data. UNODC analyses how different forms of crime converge and reinforce each other in speciﬁc regions. Spatial data have shown the convergence of criminal activities in areas such as the Sahel, Brazil and the Mekong region. Geospatial Resources Approximately 50 GIS and remote sensing staff, primarily based in ﬁeld ofﬁces, support the ICMP and other geospatial projects. UNODC uses a combination of proprietary and open-source software, including Esri products (e.g ArcGIS), along with ERDAS, PCI, QGIS, Python and R. The Ofﬁce assists United Nations Member States to establish legal and regulatory frameworks to govern space activities and strengthens the capacity of developing countries to use space science, technology and applications for development by helping to integrate space capabilities into national development programmes. Through the United Nations Programme on Space Applications, UNOOSA conducts international workshops, training courses and pilot projects on topics that include remote sensing, satellite navigation, satellite meteorology, tele-education and basic space sciences for the beneﬁt of developing nations. The International Committee on Global Navigation Satellite Systems (ICG) facilitates compatibility, interoperability and transparency between all the satellite navigation systems, to promote and protect the use of their open service applications and thereby beneﬁt the global community. UN-Space convenes annual sessions of the Inter-Agency Meeting on Outer Space Activities to discuss space-related matters among United Nations system entities. UN-Space organizes informal sessions that are open to Member States, private sector, non-governmental institutions and academia.
UNOOSA is also the United Nations focal point for satellite imagery requests during disasters and manages the United Nations Platform for Space-based Information for Disaster Management and Emergency Response (UN-SPIDER), established in 2006. The programme has the mandate to “ensure that all countries and international and regional organizations have access to and develop the capacity to use all types of space-based information to support the full disaster management cycle” .
Geospatial Data and Technology UNOOSA uses and promotes the use of free Earth observation data but is also a signatory to memoranda of understanding (MoUs) with providers of (geospatial) Earth observation data such as Airbus, DigitalGlobe/Maxar, China National Space Administration, and others in development. The satellite imagery is used for the monitoring of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), disaster risk reduction and monitoring of impacts of climate change. The Ofﬁce has access to additional Earth observation (EO) data and products through various mechanisms: as an authorized user, UNOOSA can trigger the International Charter “Space and Major Disasters” on request of government agencies; UNOOSA is a Joint Project Team member of Sentinel Asia and a user of the Copernicus EMS; it is also an active member of the International Working Group on Satellite-based Emergency Mapping (IWG-SEM) (http://www.un-spider.org/ network/iwg-sem). Geospatial Usage Geospatial data are used for disaster management and sustainable development purposes. UNOOSA promotes the use of geospatial data and tools through dedicated knowledge portals, such as the UN-SPIDER portal (http://www.un-spider.
org/), workshops and training sessions, mostly organized in countries of need. UN-SPIDER has a series of documented recommended practices that are available to practice step-by-step with satellite data in open-source geographic information system (GIS) software. UNOOSA connects data providers with data users and participates in the Group on Earth Observations (GEO) and Committee on Earth Observation Satellites (CEOS) events. 19 SECRETARIAT UNOOSA Geospatial Resources UNOOSA has two remote sensing/GIS professional staff and a pool of interns/visiting scientists that work on geospatial information and remote sensing applications. Furthermore, UNOOSA has a network of six Regional Centres for Space, Science and Technology Education and an expanding network of twenty-three Regional Support Ofﬁces (RSOs) for UN-SPIDER. The RSOs have a large number of experts in geospatial information and remote sensing and work with Earth observation data (space agencies, research centres, universities or disaster management institutions) and use their expertise to assist countries in the use of data for emergency response and disaster management. The experts from the RSOs assist at training workshops, provide training material and provide maps and data analysis at all stages of the disaster management cycle. The scope of work is in line with ECA ’s mandate to support regional priorities and initiatives. The objective is to promote and expand the use of geospatial resources (data, information and services) in decision-making processes related to sustainable development, economic growth, natural resource management, environmental protection and social progress. Appropriate geospatial data and information should also be made available to the entire community of users.
Key geospatial activities include:  Developing and maintaining purpose-driven geospatial information resources, such as spatial data, standards and tools, to support regional initiatives. This aims to improve access to and use of spatially enabled data for informed decision-making in Africa’s development agenda.  Supporting the implementation, monitoring and evaluation of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), which require geospatial datasets for evidence-based decision-making.  Assisting Member States, subregional and regional institutions in developing and integrating spatial data infrastructures and integrated geospatial information frameworks at national and regional levels.  Strengthening the integration of statistics and geospatial information by mainstreaming geospatial technology into statistical processes.  Providing technical support to subprogrammes and ECA entities to incorporate geographic information systems (GIS), remote sensing and other geoinformation tools in analysing and presenting socioeconomic data for research and policy analysis.  Advancing comprehensive geospatial information policies that align with international programmes and initiatives, including the United Nations Global Geospatial Information Management (UN-GGIM), for which ECA serves as the Secretariat for UN-GGIM: Africa.  As Secretariat of UN-GGIM: Africa, the Economic Commission for Africa (ECA) also guides Member States in developing their policies, standards and institutional and legal frameworks through the development of policy guidelines and relevant frameworks. Examples of this work include:  Development of a policy guideline for the implementation of National Spatial Data Infrastructure (NSDI).  Supporting Member States in the development and implementation of their national spatial data infrastructures.  Supporting Member States in the development and implementation of their national action plan for integrated geospatial information frameworks.  Development of a geospatial data taxonomy for use in tracking the SDGs in Africa;  Assessment of the availability of geospatial datasets for monitoring and implementing the SDGs at the national level.  Development of a Geospatial and Statistical Framework for Africa to integrate geospatial and statistical information at regional and national levels. Geospatial Data and Technology ECA sources and manages socioeconomic data and data relevant for the monitoring of SDG indicators. It is continuously building regional geospatial databases: fundamental, core datasets and thematic data for various economic sectors. Some of the regional databases include: the African component of the Second Level Administrative Boundaries (SALB) geodatabase, which compiles authoritative administrative boundaries from National Geospatial Information Authorities and a regional infrastructure geodatabase. ECA also develops web-based applications using modern web technologies and services to enhance the integration, accessibility and usability of geospatial information and statistics. It employs platforms and systems such as ArcGIS Server, ArcGIS Online and image-analysis software (e.g., ERDAS Imagine) for data management and analysis. 23 REGIONAL COMMISSIONS ECA endeavours to research and demonstrate the use of emerging technologies such as artiﬁcial intelligence, machine learning and GeoAI. It also explores open-platforms, open data and open-source software and advises and encourages Member States to adopt these tools for their geospatial and statistical work.
Geospatial Usage At ECA, geospatial information is essential to:  Maintain ECA ’s role in supporting Member States to strengthen geospatial capacity and to serve as the regional anchor for intergovernmental proceedings.6  Stay current with global United Nations trends by placing equal emphasis on geospatial information management, in line with other regional commissions and Headquarters.  Maintain momentum in supporting ECA ’s constituencies by strengthening geospatial capacity in African countries and promoting its use to address key regional and global challenges.  Ensure harmonized geospatial methods and tools through interoperable data aligned with common frameworks and standards adopted at all levels.
In addition to these institutional roles, ECA uses geospatial data in its operations to support evidence-based policymaking, research and monitoring of the SDGs. As part of its think tank function, ECA conducts research and produces thematic publications and policy briefs that include maps and other geospatial products. Flagship publications include: Economic Report on Africa (ERA), Assessing Regional Integration in Africa (ARIA) and Africa Sustainable Development Report. One example of applied use is a prototype web application developed to demonstrate the integration of geospatial and statistical data for mapping and monitoring the SDGs. 24 BLUEPRINT 2.0 GEOSPATIAL LANDSCAPE OF THE UNITED NATIONS SYSTEM Economic Commission for Europe (ECE) Geospatial Activities The United Nations Economic Commission for Europe (UNECE) has no regular funding allocated for geospatial activities, therefore it has no geospatial posts and is not able to provide secretariat support to UN-GGIM: Europe. Activities are dependent on extrabudgetary funding sources. The UNECE Statistical Division participates in global and regional initiatives, including UN-GGIM, the European Forum for Geography and Statistics (EFGS) and the Geographic Information System of the Commission (GISCO). Every two years, the Conference of European Statisticians is organized back-to-back with the UN-GGIM: Europe meeting, featuring a joint day to strengthen collaboration.
Supported by European Union funding, the Statistical Division has initiated the Integration of Geospatial and Statistical Data (INGEST) project (2023-2024) to build capacity in integrating geospatial and statistical data. Under the INGEST project, the following activities were undertaken: 1. Set-up of the UNECE Task Force on Standards Issues for Integration of Statistical and Geospatial Information publication of: A path towards the use of common standards to support the Integration of Geospatial and Statistical information (UNECE 2024) and Issues and obstacles to the greater integration of statistical and geospatial information across the UNECE region (UNECE 2024). 2. Organization of a Joint UNECE, Eurostat, UN-GGIM: Europe Workshop on the Integration of Geospatial and Statistical Data, aimed at strengthening ties between statistical and geospatial communities across the UNECE region, promoting collaboration and advancing integration through institutional partnerships and the adoption of common standards.
3. Launch of the INGEST blog series, which explores a range of data integration topics and shares guidance, resources and best practices to support data integration efforts.
4. Capacity development in integrating geospatial and statistical data: • Integrate Assessment Tool v1.0 (UNECE 2024), designed to identify current and target maturity levels across a set of dimensions. • INGEST Maturity Assessment Tool v1.0 (UNECE 2024), to assess technical capabilities for data integration, focusing on data, technical infrastructure and standards. • Country studies on the integration of geospatial and statistical data in Albania, Armenia and Kazakhstan.
The UNECE Statistical Division plans to launch a second phase of the INGEST project in 2025, with funding from the European Commission (Eurostat).
Under the Inland Transport Committee of the UNECE Transport Division, the International Transport Infrastructure Observatory (ITIO) has been established. The observatory is an innovative example of how government data on new transport infrastructure projects can be presented to ﬁnancial institutions and other donors in a transparent, comprehensive and ‘bankable’ manner. It is designed as an online platform where (a) governments ﬁnd the data to prepare, benchmark and present their transport infrastructure projects and (b) ﬁnancial institutions can consider, analyse and compare projects from a regional and international perspective to identify opportunities for ﬁnancing.
The observatory is being developed on a geographic information system (GIS) platform that provides services to users, particularly governments and international ﬁnancial institutions. This United Nations GIS centre for transport infrastructure allows users to ﬁnd and analyse data on all transport networks and nodes (roads, railways, inland waterways, ports, airports, intermodal terminals, logistics centres and border crossing points), along with data on transport corridors (length, services, missing links, schedules and tariffs). It also includes data on new transport infrastructure projects, trafﬁc and cargo ﬂows and the ratiﬁcation and implementation of international conventions and agreements.

26 BLUEPRINT 2.0 GEOSPATIAL LANDSCAPE OF THE UNITED NATIONS SYSTEM Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean (ECLAC) Geospatial Activities Since 2017 , the management of geospatial information has been systematically incorporated into the work agenda of the Statistics Division of the Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean (ECLAC), reﬂecting its growing relevance and importance within the United Nations system. This signiﬁcance is demonstrated by the active functioning of the Committee of Experts on Global Geospatial Information Management (UN-GGIM), which reports directly to the Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC) and designates the authorities of Member States’ national geospatial agencies as focal points.
This Committee of Experts prepares and disseminates guidelines on various topics, including the integration of statistical and geospatial information, the use of geospatial information to support disaster management, geospatial support for the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, land administration, maritime affairs and other related matters.
In this context, ECLAC has served since 2021 as the Technical Secretariat of the United Nations Regional Committee on Global Geospatial Information Management for the Americas (UN-GGIM: Americas). ECLAC supports the Board of Directors of UN-GGIM: Americas in the formulation, execution and monitoring of geospatial capacity strengthening projects. It also facilitates the participation of Member States in global UN-GGIM working groups, provides technical support for regional and subregional geospatial events and offers technological support for the dissemination of geospatial and statistical information. At the national level, the Statistics Division provides technical assistance on geospatial matters through projects tailored to national priorities. This includes inter-institutional workshops and coordination with national statistical ofﬁces, national geospatial agencies and other relevant organizations, to strengthen governance, develop geospatial policies and promote international standards. It also supports the development and implementation of geospatial data systems and technological tools for managing and disseminating both geospatial and statistical information. Geospatial Data and Technology ECLAC is increasingly using geospatial data to support the production of information and knowledge across its substantive areas. In line with global United Nations guidelines on integrating geospatial and statistical information, new functionalities have been added to the Comisión Económica para América Latina y el Caribe Statistical Platform (CEPALSTAT) platform to link statistical data from various sources to speciﬁc locations, enabling the representation and dissemination of geospatial layers. To maximize the use and beneﬁt of this information, ECLAC has implemented an integrated and collaborative management model based on a corporate geospatial data infrastructure. This model incorporates standardized procedures for the maintenance, integration, analysis and use of geospatial data.
This collaborative work model is implemented through the ECLAC Geospatial Platform (CEPALGEO), which includes a suite of technological tools such as catalogues, viewers and geospatial services that allow remote discovery and access to geospatial information products from both internal and external sources. CEPALGEO applies standards and protocols to support data exchange, integration and interoperability within a broad regional and global data ecosystem.
Geospatial Usage ECLAC uses geospatial information to support its efforts in promoting economic and social development across the region. These datasets, organized by themes such as society, economy, environment and cross-cutting issues, are part of its core information assets.
Geospatial data are applied in a wide range of activities, including research projects, the design of public policy instruments, monitoring platforms and technical assistance.
Success stories include the Observatory on the Economic and Social Impact of COVID-19, the Interactive Map of Cluster Initiatives and Territorial Productive Articulation, Care Maps and studies on new concepts of rurality, among others.

” FUNDS, PROGRAMMES & RESEARCH 3 34 BLUEPRINT 2.0 GEOSPATIAL LANDSCAPE OF THE UNITED NATIONS SYSTEM United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) Geospatial Activities The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) is streamlining its geospatial activities under a uniﬁed strategy informed by its data strategy, aiming to enhance governance, standards, and tools for sustainable development. Geospatial efforts span crisis response, measurement of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), biodiversity conservation, and policymaking in over 170 countries. UNDP is building a governance framework and technology stack to ensure initiatives comply with United Nations Geospatial Network standards and align with global agendas such as the Paris Agreement, and the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.
UNDP provides geographic information system (GIS) support organization-wide, harmonising decentralised GIS to reduce costs, boost data sharing, raise standards, and minimise redundancy. It maintains a GIS infrastructure, delivers training globally, and applies geospatial technologies across monitoring, disaster management, urbanisation, and recovery. Key projects include ﬂood prediction in South Sudan, GeoAI damage assessment in Gaza, Port-au-Prince, and Ukraine, storm analysis in Libya, landcover monitoring in Kosovo, and waste management in Guatemala. Partnerships, such as with UNOPS for mine risk monitoring and NASA-JPL for Ukraine recovery, further strengthen these efforts. Local GIS support from country ofﬁces underpins development work.
UNDP uses geospatial tools for biodiversity conservation and sustainable land management. The UN Biodiversity Lab (UNBL) is an open-source platform supporting national and international monitoring, reporting, and collaboration in line with the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, helping countries track biodiversity and ecosystem health, integrate national data, and meet reporting requirements.
Geospatial Data and Technology UNDP collects, manages and uses a wide variety of geospatial data to inform decision-making and support development goals, leveraging both internal platforms and external datasets. The organization is also advancing its strategy for AI, including GeoAI, and open data.
Types of Geospatial Data Collected, Managed, or Used Examples of key data types include: satellite imagery and remote sensing data, geospatial vector and raster data, ground-truth data collection, real-time location and environmental data, socioeconomic data, biodiversity data. Data Management Platforms and Systems UNDP primarily relies on: Esri products and licenses, Google Earth Engine and Gemini, Microsoft Azure (Storage Blob, Managed PostgreSQL, Container Instances, Kubernetes Cluster, Web Apps, Service Bus), open-source platforms (QGIS, GDAL, rasterio, Python, PostGIS, Apache Arrow and GitHub) GeoAI and Open Data Strategy Through 2030 GeoAI: UNDP is strengthening its geospatial data analysis with GeoAI technologies. Newly published UNDP’s AI guidelines and policies will ensure responsible, ethical use of AI for improved decision-making, predictive modelling, visualising spatial trends, and disaster response.
Open Data: UNDP is dedicated to making geospatial data open, accessible, and easy to ﬁnd. Its Geospatial platforms use open data sources to improve analysis. Additionally, UNDP ensures that its own geospatial data can be easily shared. This approach supports UNDP’s commitment to transparency and advancing data-driven solutions for sustainable development. Access to commercial datasets is supported through the Development Data Partnership (https://datapartnership.org/). Open-Source Software: UNDP uses a hybrid geospatial approach, combining open-source GIS and proprietary solutions such as Esri, Google, and Microsoft products to enhance ﬂexibility and cut costs. This integration allows UNDP to meet diverse geospatial needs efﬁciently by leveraging both open-source innovation and advanced commercial tools.
Geospatial Usage Disaster Risk Reduction and Response UNDP uses geospatial data to support early warning systems, disaster response, and preparedness. This 35 FUNDS, PROGRAMMES AND RESEARCH approach supports improved relief strategies and resilience efforts. For instance, UNDP’s pilot project in Melitopol, Ukraine, helped assess building damage and inform recovery plans with actionable data. GeoAI has also aided damage evaluation in Port-au-Prince, Haiti, and Gaza, Palestine. Tools such as the Rapid Change Assessment Tool and GeoHub dynamic layers further support the UNDP Crisis Bureau.
Monitoring and Reporting Geospatial data is crucial for tracking the SDGs. UNDP employs spatial analysis to monitor key indicators and share results via story maps and dashboards. Examples include using geospatial data for SDG 7 to evaluate electricity access, and a GIS portal in Panama that tracks projects and partnerships for SDG 17 .
Monitoring and Evaluation Geospatial data enables UNDP to monitor projects in real or near-real time, track effectiveness, and make timely adjustments. Using GIS and satellite imagery, UNDP supports project monitoring and evaluation, ensuring accountability and effective implementation. For instance, in the Lake Chad Basin, UNDP’s two-phase stabilization project aims to reduce violence and support long-term peacebuilding in Cameroon, Chad, Niger, and Nigeria. An ArcGIS Site with webmaps and dashboards was developed to enhance monitoring and coordination among stakeholders.

38 BLUEPRINT 2.0 GEOSPATIAL LANDSCAPE OF THE UNITED NATIONS SYSTEM United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) Geospatial Activities The United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA)’s mission is to deliver a world where every pregnancy is wanted, every childbirth is safe and every young person’s potential is fulﬁlled. These objectives are reﬂected in a set of indicators aligned with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and the Programme of Action of the International Conference on Population and Development (ICPD), all of which require high-quality data, particularly geospatial data, to monitor global progress.
UNFPA relies extensively on census and survey data collected across countries to assess progress and remains a key partner to National Statistical Ofﬁces in generating and analysing high-quality population data. The 2020 Census Round has seen a growing use of, and demand for, geospatial technologies to ensure data quality, identify vulnerable populations, improve resource allocation and strengthen evidence-based decision-making.
Within UNFPA ’s Programme Division, the Data, Demography and Development Branch (DDDB) has been mandated by the organization’s leadership to expand the use of geospatial data and to support the UNFPA Strategic Plan. This dedicated branch spearheads the integration of geospatial science and data-driven approaches across UNFPA ’s programmatic areas. In this regard, a range of impactful geospatial initiatives has been undertaken:  Enhancement and maintenance of the UNFPA Population Data Portal, integrating geospatial data from multiple sources to monitor key indicators across gender, health and broader population and development domains.  Support to the modernization of the 2020 Census Round in data collection, utilization and dissemination, including the incorporation of geographic information system (GIS) in census cartography, the use of GIS and satellite imagery to enhance data quality and coverage and the generation of geospatial census datasets.  Supporting countries in using population data to map geospatial inequalities and advance “leaving no one behind” , including mapping geographic access to essential sexual and reproductive health services.  Collaboration with partners to produce high-resolution population estimates in hard-to-reach areas, providing vital data for humanitarian response.  Joint Programme support to countries in strengthening national capacities to generate urban and rural statistics using the standardized Degree of Urbanization methodology, enabling globally comparable statistics and SDG monitoring, in partnership with EC-JRC, UN-Habitat, United Nations Statistics Division (UNSD) and United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF).  Mapping global population exposure and vulnerability to climate change by integrating population data, census and household survey data with climate change and diverse spatial datasets.  Development of small-area estimation methods using census, survey and geospatial data to estimate family planning indicators at the small administrative unit level.
Provision of ArcGIS licensing and geospatial capacity support to UNFPA Country Ofﬁces.

42 BLUEPRINT 2.0 GEOSPATIAL LANDSCAPE OF THE UNITED NATIONS SYSTEM United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) Geospatial Activities The United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) uses geospatial tools to strengthen data-driven decision-making, improve emergency preparedness and response, and support global development priorities, including the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Geospatial analysis informs climate resilience by assessing risks, monitoring environmental change and guiding adaptive measures. In emergencies, it enables rapid mapping of impacts, access, partner activities and infrastructure damage to direct resources where most needed. The Data and Analytics Section coordinates geospatial support for major crises, including Ukraine, Gaza and Lebanon, working closely with Country Ofﬁces to address local challenges. Across development programmes, geospatial insights help target poverty reduction and improve access to essential services, optimizing the impact of investments. With partners, UNICEF supports geo-enabled microplanning for health services and strengthens government capacity to manage core geospatial data and apply spatial analysis in health programming. Spatial analysis is integral to the MICS programme, enhancing the precision and usability of socioeconomic data collected through household surveys.
Geospatial Data and Technology UNICEF uses a wide range of geospatial data to support its diverse applications, relying on partners and open data providers to ensure global spatial datasets are integrated into internal processes. Commonly used datasets include subnational administrative boundaries, statistical indicators, facility locations (schools, health centres), population data (including high-resolution rasters), infrastructure layers (roads, ports, border crossings) and Earth observation data and derived products for climate and environmental analysis. The climate analytics team has been using Google Earth Engine and its resources to generate high-resolution child hazard data and has tested GeoAI applications to enable map-based chatbot querying that combines indicator and hazard data within a single interface.
At a corporate level, UNICEF employs a hybrid geospatial architecture that combines proprietary tools (primarily Esri) with open-source solutions. UNICEF is an active contributor to the Digital Public Goods Alliance and is developing and maintaining corporate open-source platforms such as GeoRepo, which provides harmonized administrative boundaries and core datasets, and GeoSight, which enables visualisation of subnational indicators and spatial layers. Additional open-source tools support speciﬁc use cases, for example the Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys (MICS) Geocode Plugin for QGIS for anonymizing survey cluster locations and AccessMod 5 for modelling physical accessibility to health services.
Most of UNICEF’s spatial datasets are stored in its corporate web geographic information system (GIS) platforms, including ArcGIS Online, ArcGIS Enterprise and GeoSight, with harmonized global, subnational administrative boundaries stored in the GeoRepo platform and accessible through APIs and as vector tiles. UNICEF integrates Statistical Data and Metadata eXchange (SDMX) data standards and APIs to link the Data Warehouse with GeoRepo and GeoSight, improving interoperability and automation of data pipelines, including through GitHub, Databricks and Google Earth Engine.
UNICEF is also advancing the use of SDMX as a standard for disseminating indicator data and is actively building integrations between the SDMX indicator data warehouse and geospatial platforms to ensure that statistical data can be easily mapped and visualised. Open data, open software, open standards and the responsible use of GeoAI are likely to remain key principles for guiding the future use of geospatial technology at UNICEF . Geospatial Usage UNICEF uses geospatial data to improve planning, response and monitoring across all phases of operations. Geospatial Data and Technology WFP’s services are supported by a geospatial infrastructure and tools powered by both open-source and proprietary software to:  Automate the ingestion of global climate and Earth observation (EO) data and indicators  Apply cloud computing, geostatistics and machine learning for spatial analysis  Deliver high-value geospatial products for planning, implementation and emergency response  Provide user-friendly access to climate hazard and vulnerability data through interactive dashboards  Manage standardized global geographic reference data across operations The Humanitarian Data Cube (HDC) is central to the geospatial infrastructure, providing climate and Earth observation data and indicators to support WFP , governments and humanitarian partners globally.
PRISM is a tool developed in collaboration with governments and WFP country ofﬁces. It integrates real-time hazard data (such as droughts, ﬂoods, storms and earthquakes) with food security and socioeconomic vulnerability data to support early warning, anticipatory action and response planning. PRISM is recognized as a Digital Public Good.
Geospatial Usage Support to livelihoods and resilience programmes Geospatial tools and EO data are applied to design, monitor and evaluate resilience programmes:  Asset Impact Monitoring from Space (AIMS): Assesses long-term impacts of resilience interventions (e.g., reforestation, terracing) using satellite imagery, ensuring programmes are accountable, measurable and adaptive.  Integrated Context Analysis (ICA): Combines hazard and historical food security data to inform programme design.  Climate analysis: Uses historical and projected data to understand climate impacts on food security and inform resilience strategies that reduce risk and enhance adaptive capacity.
Support to emergency operations (preparedness and response) Geospatial analytics and early warning tools enhance emergency response:  Advanced Disaster Analysis and Mapping (ADAM): Delivers near real-time alerts and disaster impact assessments (e.g., ﬂoods, cyclones, earthquakes) to guide timely and targeted humanitarian actions.  Natural hazard risk analysis: Identiﬁes high-risk areas such as ﬂoods, storms and droughts to support preparedness and planning.  Emergency mapping and analysis: Produces maps and analytics on displacement, conﬂict zones, crop conditions and infrastructure damage to support situational awareness and operational decisions.
Seasonal monitoring and climate risk applications Geospatial tools support anticipatory action and risk reduction:  Seasonal monitoring and outlooks: analyse near real-time and forecast data on droughts, ﬂoods and temperature extremes to guide contingency planning.  Trigger models for anticipatory action: Develop data-driven triggers based on seasonal forecasts to enable preventive action ahead of hazards.  Strengthening national institutions: Builds the capacity of national agencies in forecasting and monitoring climate hazards through training, tools and data access.

46 BLUEPRINT 2.0 GEOSPATIAL LANDSCAPE OF THE UNITED NATIONS SYSTEM United Nations Institute for Training and Research (UNITAR) Geospatial Activities The United Nations Satellite Centre (UNOSAT), part of the United Nations Institute for Training and Research (UNITAR), is a technology-intensive programme supporting the United Nations core objectives. As a centre of excellence for satellite imagery analysis and geographic information system (GIS) solutions, it provides geographic insight for senior decision-makers and ﬁeld workers within and outside the UN system, with special focus on Member States. UNOSAT is hosted at CERN, the European Organization for Nuclear Research. The vision of UNITAR-UNOSAT is to promote evidence-based decision-making for peace, security and resilience and its mission is to provide coordinated geospatial analysis and build capacities for the use of geoinformation technology towards achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). The strategic objectives are to:  provide coordinated geospatial analysis to the United Nations and Member States in times of crisis,  develop capacities in the use of technology towards achieving the SDGs, and  develop and promote innovative geospatial solutions for the United Nations system, its partners and Member States.
These objectives result in geospatial products and services, primarily derived from satellite imagery, for decision-makers and ﬁeld personnel within Member States and the United Nations system, as well as capacity building of national and regional actors in the use of geographic information technologies (GIT) for disaster risk reduction, sustainable development, peace and security. Typical areas of satellite imagery analysis include humanitarian relief, conﬂict analysis, environmental assessments, protection of cultural heritage, disaster risk reduction and climate resilience, human rights and sustainable development. Knowledge transfer through training and capacity development for Member States and other actors is also provided within the same thematic areas. UNOSAT serves as the focal point for geospatial activities in the Global Disaster Alert and Coordination System (GDACS), coordinated by the United Nations Ofﬁce for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), including the Satellite Mapping Coordination System (SMCS), which facilitates operational coordination of satellite mapping activities during humanitarian disasters. UNOSAT also works with partners to develop artiﬁcial intelligence models for analysing satellite imagery and extracting useful vector data.
Structure UNOSAT consists of three sections:  Disaster Risk Management and Climate Resilience Section  Human Security and Human Rights Section  Business Exploration, Strategic Planning and Coordination Section UNOSAT has its headquarters in Geneva, with ofﬁces in Bangkok, Nairobi and New York. Geospatial Data and Technology UNOSAT focuses on satellite imagery from free and open-source and commercial data, in-kind donations and from the International Charter on Space and Major Disasters. It produces derived information products from satellite imagery and related geodata, including maps, statistics, reports and geodata for direct integration in GIS systems, as well as web maps, story maps and customised products. Many of these products are available via the UNOSAT website and the Humanitarian Data Exchange (HDX), covering themes such as building damage, refugee settlements, ﬂood water extents and more.

UNOPS delivers technical expertise, operational platforms and advisory support to a wide range of United Nations missions and national authorities, often in high-risk and post-conﬂict settings. IMAT leads geospatial innovation within UNOPS, developing practical tools with leading research institutions such as the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), École polytechnique fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL) and Carnegie Mellon University to assess infrastructure damage, prioritize recovery and monitor delivery in fragile and crisis-affected contexts.
Key Geospatial Functions:  Infrastructure damage assessments: UNOPS conducts infrastructure damage assessments through integrated satellite, geographic information system (GIS) and AI approaches, combining pre- and post-disaster imagery, change detection and AI classiﬁcation to quantify physical damage, prioritize redevelopment and inform recovery proposals.  Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)-linked spatial analysis: UNOPS performs this analysis across its projects and development needs to guide investment targeting in least developed countries and fragile states.  Risk estimation of explosive ordnance (EO): Using AI models and data from the EO sector and the Humanitarian Data Exchange (HDX), UNOPS estimates the risk of EO to support humanitarian mine action prioritization and socioeconomic impact assessments. UNOPS has developed an AI-driven spatial analysis model for Myanmar mine action prioritization to identify high-risk areas based on population exposure and access constraints. A machine learning-based model for Afghanistan estimates landmine contamination in non-surveyed areas.  Integrated spatial dashboards: UNOPS uses integrated spatial dashboards for planning, monitoring and reporting, which include contract quality monitoring dashboards that integrate contract data with geospatial outputs to improve accountability and ﬁeld delivery.  Capacity-building: UNOPS provides capacity-building for partners in ﬁeld-based GIS and remote sensing, including training for government and UN partners such as the United Nations Mine Action Service (UNMAS), the United Nations Ofﬁce of Counter-Terrorism (UNOCT) and the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP). Geospatial Data and Technology UNOPS has built a suite of cloud-native tools that process and visualise spatial data across operational contexts, often in collaboration with national actors and ﬁeld teams. Key systems and data types include:  UNOPS Infrastructure Monitoring Toolkit: This toolkit aggregates global disaster alerts (e.g., GDACS, NASA) and analyses them alongside UNOPS assets and past projects to guide response and investment.  Damage Assessment Framework: This framework combines pre- and post-disaster imagery, change detection and AI classiﬁcation to quantify physical damage, prioritize redevelopment and inform recovery proposals.  Spatial Dashboards: Dashboards integrate contract data with geospatial outputs to improve accountability and ﬁeld delivery. Examples include the Gaza Mine Action prioritization mapping application, which provides real-time access to relevant decision-making data for explosive ordnance disposal (EOD) ofﬁcers and the UNMAS UN GeoPortal IED Dashboard for reporting and analysis of mine action activities across multiple country programs.  RELand (Risk Estimation of Landmines): An AI-based system that uses HDX, ACLED and remote sensing data to spatially estimate EO risk for planning and prioritization. ” SPECIALIZED AGENCIES 4 60 BLUEPRINT 2.0 GEOSPATIAL LANDSCAPE OF THE UNITED NATIONS SYSTEM Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) Geospatial Activities The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) is a specialized agency of the United Nations that leads international efforts to defeat hunger. With 195 members (194 countries and the European Union) FAO has worked since 1945 in over 130 countries worldwide. Headquartered in Rome, Italy, FAO is present in over 130 countries. Article 1 of its constitution requires FAO to “collect, analyse, interpret and disseminate information related to nutrition, food and agriculture” . Given the inherent spatial dimension of agricultural activities, geospatial solutions are a critical enabler for the Organization to achieve its mandate and support its Members in the transformation to more efﬁcient, inclusive, resilient and sustainable agrifood systems. FAO, as a custodian agency of twenty-one indicators across six Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), supports its Members in data collection and reporting, including using geospatial tools. This is done through direct measurements, for example, of forest cover, land use changes or water consumption in agriculture, by supporting survey design and the disaggregation of data at the subnational level to inform decision-making processes. Geospatial Data and Technology Georeferenced data and information are collected and used across FAO departments and decentralised ofﬁces worldwide. The FAO agro-informatics platform integrates information technology with earth observation, remote sensing, agricultural data management, analysis and application to deliver reliable, timely, high-resolution, documented, integrated location-based information and analysis across diverse sectors and various sources. The platform includes FAO’s catalogue of geospatial data. The default FAO data license is Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0). The platform is built on open-source technologies and is a digital public good. Initially designed to support the Hand-in-Hand Initiative, it has grown to become a powerful tool for delivering FAO’s work and achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly SDG 1 (No Poverty) and SDG 2 (Zero Hunger). It underpins many FAO applications catering to speciﬁc thematic and regional communities, including market-based transformation of agrifood systems, water data, animal disease management, climate-smart agriculture, crop production early warning, ecosystem restoration, globally federated integrated soil data, land cover, crop type mapping, crop calendar, phenology and smallholder advisory services. The platform offers rich data exploration features, including search and explore, time-series analysis, data comparison across locations and periods, visualisation, geospatial analysis, reports and stories. The platform has a thriving community with rapid growth in users and data. Currently, 175,000 users from 186 countries generate approximately twenty billion requests across two million layers and 5,000 datasets federated from one hundred organizations. 61 SPECIALIZED AGENCIES Geospatial Resources Geospatial applications are widely adopted in FAO for monitoring food security and agriculture, including forestry, ﬁshery and across disciplines, including socioeconomic and statistical domains. The Geospatial Unit in the Land and Water Division includes three staff and seventeen consultants, while the Agro-Informatics team in the IT Division includes four staff and twelve consultants. Other geospatial hubs with specialised skills are hosted in other departments and divisions, including Forestry, Fishery and Economy Departments and the Ofﬁce of Climate Change. Including regional and country ofﬁces, there are more than twenty-ﬁve staff and one hundred consultants worldwide. The Organization has developed and maintains a wide range of geospatial tools, including land cover metalanguage and classiﬁcation standards, cloud-based image analysis processing for forest resources monitoring, crop suitability and production assessment, livestock environmental assessment models, early warning for agricultural droughts and many more. Its easy-to-use interface, powered by cloud-based supercomputers, offers unparalleled satellite data access, supporting improved climate change mitigation and data-driven land-use policies. 62 BLUEPRINT 2.0 GEOSPATIAL LANDSCAPE OF THE UNITED NATIONS SYSTEM International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) Geospatial Activities The International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) is a specialized agency of the United Nations, headquartered in Montreal, Canada, with seven regional ofﬁces worldwide (Bangkok, Cairo, Dakar, Lima, Mexico, Nairobi and Paris). It was established by Member States in 1944 to administer and govern the Convention on International Civil Aviation (commonly referred to as the “Chicago Convention”). ICAO serves as the global forum for States on international civil aviation. It develops global Standards and Recommended Practices (SARPs), including guidance material, conducts safety oversight and compliance audits, performs studies and analyses of the air transport market, provides technical assistance to Member States and builds aviation capacity through cooperation among its Member States and stakeholders. ICAO maintains several geospatial datasets related to aviation, including but not limited to, lists of airports used for international civil aviation (location indicators), airport safety characteristics, airspace delineation, aviation routes and ﬁve-letter name codes for the identiﬁcation of signiﬁcant points and designators for air trafﬁc service (ATS) routes. ICAO maintains an aeronautical geographic information system (GIS) function within the Air Navigation Bureau (ANB) which responds to requests for maps and other geospatial services, including regional air navigation plans, crisis response and contingency mapping for situations affecting or involving civil aviation and geospatial analysis such as air trafﬁc growth, emissions estimation based on known trafﬁc schedules and performance measurements of regional and global civil aviation.
