64 BLUEPRINT 2.0 GEOSPATIAL LANDSCAPE OF THE UNITED NATIONS SYSTEM International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD) Geospatial Activities The International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD) is an international ﬁnancial institution and a specialised agency of the United Nations, based in Rome, Italy. IFAD provides ﬁnancial resources to national governments for agricultural programmes that promote rural development. There are two main ways in which geospatial data and technology are used at IFAD:  Design of country strategies and investment projects, where geospatial information is used to identify vulnerable communities and areas in which the Fund wishes to invest.  Monitoring and impact evaluation, where location-speciﬁc data on investments and smallholders is collected during project implementation and completion. This data are used to monitor project progress and assess impact.
Geospatial Data and Technology IFAD’s design and evaluation teams use a wide range of external geospatial datasets to inform project design and assess impact. These include administrative boundaries, environmental, climate and socioeconomic datasets from a variety of providers. To manage and analyse these data, geographic information system (GIS) analysts at IFAD primarily use QGIS and ArcGIS platforms.
IFAD manages two types of geodata related to its operations. First, it produces a map for each project showing the administrative areas in which the project operates. These maps are also the basis on which IFAD reports the locations of its projects to the International Aid Transparency Initiative (IATI). Second, IFAD is increasingly collecting investment-level data, such as the location of markets, irrigation schemes or rural roads in which the Fund invests. This data is used for monitoring, impact evaluation and other operational purposes.
IFAD has developed an internal repository for geospatial data based on open-source technologies, including PostgreSQL/ PostGIS, GeoServer, Geonode and OpenLayers. It provides web-map and web dashboard functionality. IFAD users can store and access GIS ﬁles in different formats. IFAD has also developed an innovative GIS data delivery application called GeoScan, which provides access to over 180 different layers from major data providers. In addition, IFAD has developed a custom widget solution to integrate large volumes of geospatial data into Microsoft Power BI applications.
The Fund is currently developing a mobile application to collect and verify georeferenced ﬁeld-level data from its operations, enabling deeper insights into its impact on rural poverty and the environment.
IFAD has an in-house artiﬁcial intelligence (AI) development platform that combines many technologies to support multiple use cases, from machine learning for advanced analytics to generative AI for knowledge management. IFAD has several open-source projects available on platforms such as GitHub, incorporating contributions to and from open-source communities and developers.
The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and IFAD are jointly developing the Adaptation, Biodiversity and Carbon Mapping (ABC-Map) tool, a geospatial application for analysing adaptation, biodiversity, land-use change and carbon.
The Fund is expected to award a grant to a public foundation to compile spatial, satellite-derived datasets on a wide range of topics for use in project design, implementation, monitoring and evaluation and impact assessment. These datasets will be publicly available.
IFAD is ﬁnancing a project (CAPEO) with the OpenGeoHub Foundation to compile spatial, satellite-derived datasets on a wide range of topics for use in project design, implementation, monitoring and evaluation and impact assessment, in partnership with Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and the World Food Programme (WFP). These datasets will be publicly available. The ILO became the ﬁrst specialized agency of the United Nations in 1946. The main aims of the ILO are to promote rights at work, encourage decent employment opportunities, enhance social protection and strengthen dialogue on work-related issues. As the only tripartite UN agency, the ILO brings together governments, employers and workers of 187 Member States to set labour standards, develop policies and design programmes promoting decent work for all women and men.
The ILO conducts geospatial activities, primarily through the STRENGTHEN2 project (Employment Impact Assessment to Maximize Job Creation in Africa). Co-ﬁnanced by the European Union, the project aims to assess the employment impacts of infrastructure investments in sub-Saharan Africa. It applies a range of methods to estimate both direct and indirect employment effects of projects. To assess the long-term impacts of investments, the ILO uses geographic information system (GIS) and remote sensing to measure the economic and employment effects of infrastructure and agricultural projects. Assessments using these geospatial methods have been conducted in Rwanda, Kenya, Zambia and Malawi. Beyond this, additional work on impact assessment within the ILO Employment Policy Department utilises spatial data to analyse the impacts of natural disasters, conﬂicts, labour productivity and inequality. The ILO’s 2025 Reference Guide on Employment Impact Assessment highlights GIS and remote sensing as increasingly essential tools for conducting Employment Impact Assessments (EmpIAs).
Georeferenced information is also disseminated through reports and dashboards, primarily via ILOSTAT , the ILO’s central portal for labour statistics. The ILO also compiles and makes available legal databases comprising labour laws, standards and policies from all Member States. These resources are often georeferenced and disseminated through reports, dynamic web pages and dashboards. Finally, multiple departments and ofﬁces collect a range of quality and impact indicators from programmes and projects worldwide. These are presented through dashboards that provide information on ILO development cooperation spending (DC Dashboard) across the globe, the evaluation process (i-eval Discovery) and the results achieved (IR Dashboard).
Geospatial Data and Technology The work on employment impact assessment utilises a range of geospatial and survey data:  Survey data: Census, household surveys and labour force surveys collect administrative data to produce national statistics on employment and shed light on the structure of the labour force. Labour force surveys, usually collected from a sample of individuals that are nationally representative, aim to capture the number of jobs and the characteristics of these jobs. This information can be used to track progress and for monitoring and planning purposes.  Satellite imagery: The use of satellite images in combination with algorithms can be used to monitor and evaluate projects over time.  Night-time lights satellite data: Night-light data are the amount of light at night that can be observed from outer space. Based on previous research, this can be applied as a proxy for GDP at the local level. This is particularly valuable in countries with under-resourced statistical systems.
Geospatial Usage GIS is applied under the STRENGTHEN2 project and within the Employment Policy Department to conduct the following analyses:  Night-time lights analysis to assess the impacts of transport projects, conﬂicts, natural disasters and inequality. Changes in light intensity before and after an event or project are analysed as a proxy for economic activity (GDP), which can be translated into estimated changes in employment at the local level and over time.  Labour force survey integration, combining employment information with geographic data, enables analysis of changes in employment outcomes before and International Labour Organization (ILO) 67 SPECIALIZED AGENCIES after project completion. STRENGTHEN2 applies this approach to assess the employment impacts of roads and agricultural projects, using a difference-in-differences econometric approach.  Satellite data analysis is used to monitor land-use change and agricultural productivity. Environmental indices derived from satellite imagery can be compared over time to assess the severity of events such as droughts or the impacts of irrigation schemes. This information is combined with survey data to assess impacts on jobs and livelihoods.  Accessibility analysis, using GIS, evaluates how road projects have improved access to services, such as education, health and markets, which in turn can support positive employment outcomes.
In addition to the STRENGTHEN2 project, the ILO has established a Geospatial Services Hub to provide access to geospatial data, cartography and mapping services for internal users. The Hub supports the production of ofﬁcial maps for all ILO publications, based on the latest version of the United Nations global cartography.
Geospatial Resources The ILO has dedicated resources for geospatial activities under the STRENGTHEN2 project, including a staff GIS specialist responsible for coordinating the GIS work. Additional colleagues within the Employment Policy Department also use geospatial data in their work. More broadly, specialists at headquarters and in ﬁeld ofﬁces contribute to the design and production of choropleth maps and other map-based visualisations. Field ofﬁces also support Member States in systematising georeferenced information to support the production of reports.

Its instruments, standards and reporting mechanisms support the collection, exchange and use of location-based maritime information:  Safety of navigation and emergency response. IMO adopts ships’ routeing measures and mandatory ship reporting systems under SOLAS, including trafﬁc separation schemes, deep-water routes, precautionary areas and areas to be avoided. It also establishes requirements for search and rescue (SAR), the Global Maritime Distress and Safety System (GMDSS), Long-range Identiﬁcation and Tracking (LRIT) and Electronic Chart Display and Information Systems (ECDIS).  Digital maritime information. With the International Hydrographic Organization (IHO) and other standards bodies, IMO supports e-navigation, application of S-100 standards in ECDIS, interoperable digital maritime services and alignment between S-100 and the IMO Compendium on Facilitation and Electronic Business.  Marine environmental protection. Geospatial information supports Particularly Sensitive Sea Areas (PSSAs) and associated protective measures; MARPOL Special Areas and Emission Control Areas; ballast-water exchange areas and warnings; port reception facilities; and reporting on dumping sites, permits and monitoring under the London Convention and Protocol.  Global reporting and analysis. Member States report location-based information through IMO systems on marine casualties, piracy and armed robbery, maritime security, SAR and GMDSS services, ballast-water measures and port reception facilities. IMO-commissioned studies and impact assessments have also used external vessel-activity and Automatic Identiﬁcation System (AIS) data.  Together, these activities support IMO’s contribution to SDG 14 as well as elements of SDGs 9, 13 and 17 .
Geospatial Data & Technologies IMO instruments and reporting systems encompass geospatially referenced information including ship routeing measures and reporting-system limits; SAR regions and rescue coordination centres; GMDSS facilities; Particularly Sensitive Sea Areas (PSSAs) and MARPOL Special Areas; port reception facilities; casualty and piracy incident locations; dumping-site information; and LRIT ship-position information. Much of this information is submitted by Member States or Contracting Parties under IMO instruments and reporting procedures. Access to LRIT information is governed by SOLAS and the related LRIT technical documentation.
Core platforms and standards. The Global Integrated Shipping Information System (GISIS) is IMO’s comprehensive online hub for collecting, processing and sharing shipping-related data, with publicly accessible and restricted-access modules. LRIT provides global identiﬁcation and tracking of ships, supported by technical speciﬁcations covering data security and information exchange. IMO works with IHO on S-100 in ECDIS and e-navigation, while the IMO Compendium supports harmonized and interoperable exchange between ships, ports, Maritime Single Windows and public authorities.
Direction. IMO is upgrading GISIS following analysis of current operations and future data-management needs. Related work includes application of S-100 in ECDIS, an IP-based S-100 data-distribution framework, continued development of the IMO Compendium and further development of the IMO Strategy on Maritime Digitalization.
Geospatial Usage Geospatial information deﬁnes where maritime requirements and protective measures apply; supports voyage planning, navigation, distress communication and SAR coordination; and informs analysis, regulatory proposals and impact assessments. IMO-adopted geographic measures are published in IMO instruments and incorporated, as appropriate, into ofﬁcial charts and digital navigation products by national hydrographic authorities.

70 BLUEPRINT 2.0 GEOSPATIAL LANDSCAPE OF THE UNITED NATIONS SYSTEM International Telecommunication Union (ITU) Geospatial Activities The International Telecommunication Union (ITU) is the United Nations specialized agency for information and communication technologies (ICTs). ITU allocates global radio spectrum and satellite orbits, develops the technical standards that ensure networks and technologies interconnect seamlessly and strives to improve access to ICTs for underserved communities worldwide. The ITU Secretariat is composed of a General Secretariat and three bureaus: the Radiocommunication Bureau (BR), the Development Bureau (BDT) and the Standardization Bureau (TSB). The ITU does not currently have a geospatial section or department. However, several staff in ITU, from different bureaus, work with geospatial data, both as developers and users. Recognizing the importance of geospatial information management, the ITU established an intersectoral team in May 2019 under the supervision of the ITU Deputy Secretary-General. This team, working in cooperation with geospatial partners such as the United Nations Geospatial Network, the World Geospatial Industry Council and the Open Geospatial Consortium, aims to leverage geospatial data to support the development of telecommunication infrastructure and systems to advance the ITU’s mission. 72 BLUEPRINT 2.0 GEOSPATIAL LANDSCAPE OF THE UNITED NATIONS SYSTEM United Nations Educational, Scientifc and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) Geospatial Activities Created on 16 November 1945, the United Nations Educational, Scientiﬁc and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) is the United Nations’ organization for education, the sciences and culture. Its Constitution, drafted in the aftermath of World War II, opens with the following words, a road map for the Organization: “Since wars begin in the minds of men, it is in the minds of men that the defences of peace must be constructed” . More than 70 years after UNESCO’s foundation, this vision of peace remains deeply relevant. It is, moreover, an essential condition for achieving sustainable development. UNESCO fosters dialogue and mutual understanding between peoples through education, the sharing of different cultures and the free circulation of ideas and knowledge.
Because of its complex mandate, UNESCO operates in multiple areas of geospatial activity, in relation to education, culture, sciences, freedom of expression and access to information. Approximately 10 million square kilometres of the Earth’s surface are now protected by UNESCO designated sites such as Biosphere Reserves, Global Geoparks and World Heritage sites and thousands of items inscribed in lists are geo-localized.
For example, some of the activities within the culture sector involve satellite monitoring of World Heritage properties to support the monitoring of these sites, enabling local authorities to identify potential threats, such as land use changes, which could place the sites in danger and thereby provide sufﬁcient time for authorities to develop and implement mitigation strategies. The World Heritage Online Map Platform represents a geodatabase of all 1,000+ World Heritage properties with near real-time monitoring. These data are then overlapped with data from other programs such as the Man and the Biosphere and the UNESCO Geoparks Network. Such tools directly contribute to the implementation of the 2030 Agenda, in particular to the achievement of Goal 11, Target 11.4: “Strengthen efforts to protect and safeguard the world’s cultural and natural heritage” .
Other important ongoing projects dedicated to the collection of geographical information are the International Hydrological Programme (IHP) Water Information Network System (WINS) online platform, an open-access online library and networking hub. For water, the UNESCO Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission Tsunami Programme also maintains the Tsunami Early Warning Systems (EWS) and is part of a global initiative that aims to build a complete map of the ocean ﬂoor by 2030.
Furthermore, UNESCO recently joined forces with the European Union (EU) community of scientists and practitioners to develop innovative solutions for strengthening resilience, via the development of several ICT platforms.
Geospatial Data and Technology While UNESCO applies and endorses open data policies whenever possible, it does not yet provide a single place where all geospatial-related data can be accessed. Each project provides its own data access policy. This is the case for the above mentioned projects and others. For example, the Landslide-EVO (Environmental Virtual Observatory) project, an international collaborative research initiative that demonstrated how the use of citizen science and advanced low-cost ICTs helped to develop a demand-responsive framework for landslide disaster risk reduction in the Karnali River Basin of Western Nepal, has developed participatory methods for augmenting geospatial hydrometeorological datasets in the mountains. The World Network of Biosphere Reserves holds the georeferenced data of all biosphere reserves and the Ibero-American and Caribbean Biosphere Reserves Network (IberoMAB) has the shapeﬁles of all its afﬁliated biosphere reserves. The same information is available for the 241 UNESCO Global Geoparks items.
The World Heritage Centre collects, produces, veriﬁes and manages vector layers reﬂecting the boundaries and buffer zones of World Heritage properties and speciﬁc datasets on threats to properties, including daily active ﬁres detected by VIIRS sensors (NASA) and recent earthquake data from the PAGER system.
Geospatial data collection is being used to inform emergency planning and management of natural hazards and disasters with the UNESCO G-WADI Geoserver application, which uses an artiﬁcial neural network algorithm to estimate real-time precipitation worldwide.
73 SPECIALIZED AGENCIES Some other UNESCO initiatives neither collect nor publish their own georeferenced data, as geospatial data are often provided by national authorities with restrictions. In the ﬁeld of education, for example, geospatial data on schools comes mainly from the ministries of education; cartographic and spatial data layers are obtained mainly from free database platforms; at the end of the process, georeferenced educational data are made available on the UNESCO website and on other different specialised platforms such as the Ofﬁce for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) Humanitarian Data Exchange (HDX), Armed Conﬂict Location and Event Data Project (ACLED), International Organization for Migration Displacement Tracking Matrix (IOM–DTM), United States Geological Survey (USGS), NASA and United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP).
Geospatial Usage UNESCO makes use of geospatial data in a number of different areas. For education, for example, geospatial information is used at the International Institute for Educational Planning for micro-planning and school mapping in Member States, for climate risk and vulnerability analyses in crisis-sensitive planning and for supporting policy dialogue, including between host and refugee communities.
In culture, geospatial information is part of daily monitoring activities, such as UNITAR’s UNOSAT programme that has been supporting the humanitarian community with analysis derived from satellite imagery. This is also helping the work UNESCO carries out in the Middle East region, including efforts to report on the looting of cultural artefacts. The World Heritage Committee has called upon States Parties to use satellite imagery to monitor the state of conservation of World Heritage properties. For example, results have already been reported on a number of sites facing imminent threats, ranging from wildﬁres and sea-level rise to armed conﬂict, including The Historic Centre of Odesa in Ukraine, Baalbek and Tyre in Lebanon, Pantanal Conservation Area in Brazil and Noel Kempff Mercado National Park in Bolivia.
Geospatial Resources UNESCO is sharing its geospatial tools for educational planning on free open-source platforms such as UNESDOC (for reports), QGIS (for plugins), GitLab (for codes) and HDX (for data).

74 BLUEPRINT 2.0 GEOSPATIAL LANDSCAPE OF THE UNITED NATIONS SYSTEM United Nations Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO) Geospatial Activities The United Nations Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO) promotes inclusive and sustainable industrialization, innovation and resilient infrastructure in support of the 2030 Agenda and Sustainable Development Goal 9 (SDG 9).
Within this mandate, UNIDO applies geospatial technologies to map and analyse industrial ecosystems, supply chains and infrastructure resilience.
Through its collaboration with UNITAR–UNOSAT , UNIDO has employed satellite imagery and geospatial damage-assessment mapping to support post-crisis industrial recovery, most notably for the Gaza Industrial Estate and surrounding industrial facilities.
In 2025, UNIDO launched the Compass Platform, a digital mapping system displaying its global projects, ﬁeld ofﬁces and results, further embedding geospatial intelligence into programme management, transparency and results-based reporting. Featured projects on the platform demonstrate UNIDO’s use of satellite, drone and geographic information system (GIS) technologies in industrial and environmental initiatives. In Namibia, the Promoting Sustainable Bush-Processing Value Chains project applied satellite and drone imagery with machine learning to map invasive Acacia bush, estimate biomass and guide sustainable harvesting for charcoal and feed production. In Venezuela, the Industrial Upgrading and Modernization Programme used drone and satellite monitoring of maize crops to assess plant health and soil conditions, enabling targeted fertilizer application and improved yields.
These efforts strengthen UNIDO’s capacity to integrate spatial analysis into industrial policy, crisis response and digital transformation strategies across its Member States.
Geospatial Data and Technology UNIDO’s Compass Platform serves as a centralized geospatial data interface. It visualises the organization’s project portfolios and thematic focus areas, integrating statistical indicators from the UNIDO Statistics Portal.
Replacing the former Open Data Portal, the platform enables users to explore industrial data geographically, ﬁlter results by region or thematic area and access programmatic insights.
In ﬁeld operations, UNIDO leverages satellite imagery and geospatial analysis products, such as those developed by UNOSAT’s Emergency Mapping Service, to assess industrial infrastructure, monitor damage and inform reconstruction planning.
Industrial, energy and environmental datasets collected through technical cooperation projects and Member State reporting are increasingly being georeferenced or spatially visualised to support evidence-based policymaking.
Geospatial Usage UNIDO’s geospatial applications extend across several domains:  Industrial Resilience and Crisis Response: Spatial mapping of industrial zones and facilities supports damage assessments, business-continuity planning and resilient recovery in disaster-affected regions.  Programme Monitoring and Transparency: The Compass Platform enables Member States and partners to visualise project coverage and outcomes, strengthening accountability and knowledge sharing.  Sustainable Value Chains and Eco-Industrial Parks: Mapping industrial clusters, logistics corridors and eco-industrial parks is increasingly reﬂected in UNIDO’s digitalization and circular-economy strategies.  Policy Support and Member State Advisory: Spatially enabled datasets enhance industrial diagnostics, infrastructure planning and the monitoring of SDG 9 indicators. 75 SPECIALIZED AGENCIES Geospatial Resources  UNIDO Mandate and Network: Provides institutional context, including UNIDO’s global ﬁeld operations and their role in applying geospatial approaches.  UNOSAT Collaboration: Offers satellite imagery and rapid-mapping services for industrial-recovery planning.  Compass Platform: Interactive geospatial map and analytics portal showcasing UNIDO’s programmes, projects and ofﬁces worldwide.  UNIDO Statistics Portal: Comprehensive database of industrial and trade indicators suitable for geospatial integration.  Regional Outlook Reports: Highlight industrial hubs, clusters and digital-transformation initiatives with spatial dimensions.

76 BLUEPRINT 2.0 GEOSPATIAL LANDSCAPE OF THE UNITED NATIONS SYSTEM Universal Postal Union (UPU) Geospatial Activities The global postal sector is navigating a signiﬁcant transformation, transitioning from its traditional mail delivery roots towards a dynamic, technologically driven ecosystem. This shift is underpinned by the use of digital technologies to enhance inclusion, improve sustainability and foster collaboration across the sector. The future of postal services is envisioned to be highly integrated within the digital economy, marked by advanced operational efﬁciencies, customer-centric services and a signiﬁcant contribution to societal and environmental goals.
The Universal Postal Union (UPU) works to advance a sustainable and inclusive postal sector, by supporting the digital transformation of postal operators to improve access to basic services for all, including guaranteed postal services. As part of its development policies, the integration and use of geospatial technologies within the postal sector is also included. Some examples are:  Supporting Member States in integrating geographic information system (GIS), satellite imagery and geospatial databases into postal addressing to better identify delivery points and collecting addresses and postcode data in a universal database to optimize operations, enhance efﬁciency and improve service delivery, from dynamic routing to customer service platforms.  Leveraging the global network of over 650,000 post ofﬁces for digital inclusion through the Connect Post initiative, which equips post ofﬁces with high-speed internet, digital training capabilities and the capacity to deliver essential digital services such as e-government, especially to underconnected rural and remote populations.  Gathering information and detecting major corridors of drug trafﬁcking and dangerous goods in international postal trafﬁc, and developing tools to identify parcels likely to contain dangerous goods, using machine learning and artiﬁcial intelligence (AI) trained on current and historical data to generate real-time risk scores.  Maintaining the UPU GIS database of postal events, which holds essential datasets to the organization’s work, such as international ﬁnancial systems, the customs declaration system, the world’s largest database of ofﬁcial postage stamps, or the Express Mail Service system.  Providing support on preparedness and disaster risk management to postal personnel and participating in the joint Global Initiative on AI for Natural Disaster Management  Delivering GIS training to Member States to enhance geospatial skills across its members while promoting the digitalization of the postal sector.  Leveraging international postal, aviation and trade data in a consolidated, AI-enhanced Uniﬁed Data Platform to enable a more accurate statistical measurement of cross-border e-commerce ﬂows and the impacts of logistical constraints, while contributing to the effective decarbonization of international logistics.  Fostering sustainable practices in the postal sector, from green logistics to eco-friendly packaging and promoting social and ﬁnancial inclusion for economic progress. Geospatial Data and Technology Geospatial work within UPU, as transversal infrastructure, is relatively new. To date, a variety of open-source and proprietary tools have been used by different programmes on an ad hoc basis. However, understanding and responding to the evolving postal environment requires accessible and reliable interconnected data. For this reason, the UPU is developing a transversal GIS infrastructure, in cooperation with other UN agencies, to support the use of a mapping platform, satellite imagery and geospatial analysis. UPU’s datasets integrating geospatial information vary in form and nature and comprise information on:  Standardized and interoperable postal address information, integrating administrative boundaries (levels 1 and 2) and postcodes of Member States;  Postal network mapping and service delivery levels, allowing cross-border mail track and trace, routing optimization and delivery efﬁciency;  Greenhouse gas emissions mapping; and  Postal dangerous goods search tool. 77 SPECIALIZED AGENCIES Geospatial Usage The integration of geospatial data and technology within UPU would support the optimal functioning of the international postal service supply chain and the smooth exchange of electronic data throughout the interna tional supply chain, facilitating a seamless experience for postal operators and customers worldwide. This effort is based on the need for greater coherence in the application and sharing of geospatial postal data to manage and measure the cross-border postal network activities, to better contribute to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
At UPU, some examples include address data collection and management for efﬁcient delivery of mail and parcels, route optimization, network planning, postal assets management, postal service planning, based on customer needs and service demand, performance monitoring based on universal service obligation, delivery times, satisfaction and quality of service indicators, e-commerce and monitor the carbon footprint of the postal sector. The World Health Organization (WHO) has applied geospatial technologies through the development of tools, such as HealthMapper, widely adopted by Ministries of Health and used for disease surveillance in the 1990s. Geospatial data and techniques play a central role in monitoring progress and providing a robust evidence base for policymaking in support of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and the General Programme of Work (GPW13) Triple Billion targets. Many SDGs rely on geographic information system (GIS) technologies to analyse spatial distribution and patterns, enabling the tracking of risk factors, strengthening of health information systems and support for disease prevention and control. GIS is also applied in monitoring water quality and sanitation; planning and tracking vaccination campaigns (e.g., polio, routine immunization, outbreaks); managing the distribution of health commodities (e.g., bed nets for malaria); responding to health emergencies; and addressing neglected tropical diseases and antimicrobial resistance. In addition, geospatial approaches contribute to advancing health equity through health facility mapping and more efﬁcient resource allocation (SDGs 3, 6, 13, 16).
Extending the reach of geospatial information across the Organization and beyond supports efforts to reach the most vulnerable populations ﬁrst. GIS can be used to detect social and economic inequalities within and across countries and to connect maps, applications, data and people in ways that enable more timely and informed decision-making by countries and partners.
WHO is positioned to provide coherent, comprehensive and collaborative geospatial solutions to countries and partners through:  Increasing the efﬁcient use of GIS by Member States and partners  Strengthening compliance and stewardship with WHO Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) for mapping and web-based GIS applications  Promoting a geospatial culture and community of practice through training and technical expertise in innovative technologies, application methods and mapping  Strengthening country and regional capacity in data, analytics and health information systems to meet demand and maximize population health outcomes Geospatial Data and Technology WHO has played a leading role in the development of the United Nations Second Administrative Level Boundaries (SALB) programme for over a decade. The organization maintains signiﬁcant geospatial assets, including administrative boundaries, population datasets and health administrative units. WHO has developed base maps with geographical names and boundaries consistent with WHO legal guidance. These cloud-hosted base maps are available for integration into WHO web and mobile GIS applications in multiple vector tile formats and across all six ofﬁcial United Nations languages.
Speciﬁc health datasets containing patient information, including location, are maintained on WHO servers, with geospatial data management aligned with established data privacy policies. Additional operational datasets and satellite imagery are hosted and maintained within WHO’s cloud-based Enterprise GIS platform (https://who.maps.
arcgis.com), with selected datasets available as open data.
Geospatial Usage Geospatial information is critical in health emergencies and is widely used by WHO Health Emergencies (WHE) Programme for situation dashboards, analysis and rapid assessments. It has been central to responses to outbreaks including cholera, Zika, Ebola, COVID-19 and Mpox. Geospatially enabled workﬂows include ﬁeld data collection, dashboard development, data analysis, geospatial data management, open data sharing, conﬁguration of web applications and collaboration with partners. During WHO’s recent reform process, the need for improved access to GIS technology was identiﬁed, leading to the implementation of the Enterprise GIS platform, 79 SPECIALIZED AGENCIES which is now widely used across country and regional ofﬁces. WHO Regional Ofﬁces for Africa and Europe have established dedicated GIS centres, with additional centres under development. Online GIS platforms now engage over 2,000 WHO staff and partners in health programmes, while desktop GIS tools are used by more than 1,000 staff. Capacity strengthening remains an ongoing priority.
Geospatial Resources People: WHO staff with expertise in geospatial information management, application development and analysis are distributed across the Organization, with notable concentrations in polio, health emergencies, information management and technology and data, analytics and delivery for impact, including the WHO GIS Centre for Health (GISC). WHO 80 BLUEPRINT 2.0 GEOSPATIAL LANDSCAPE OF THE UNITED NATIONS SYSTEM World Meteorological Organization (WMO) Overview The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) is the United Nations system’s authoritative voice on the state and behaviour of the Earth’s atmosphere, its interactions with land and oceans, the weather and climate it produces and the resulting distribution of water resources.
As weather, climate and the water cycle know no national boundaries, international cooperation at a global scale is essential for the development of meteorology and operational hydrology and for realizing the beneﬁts of their application. WMO provides the framework for such cooperation among its 193 Member States and Territories.
Geospatial Activities A cornerstone of WMO’s mission is to support its Members in developing, operating and enhancing worldwide systems for observing and exchanging meteorological and related data. Three core systems underpin these efforts: the WMO Integrated Global Observing System (WIGOS), the WMO Integrated Processing and Prediction Systems (WIPPS) and the WMO Information System (WIS).
The World Meteorological Organization also co-sponsors the Global Climate Observing System (GCOS). GCOS expert panels maintain deﬁnitions of Essential Climate Variables (ECVs), many of which are geospatial and are required to systematically observe Earth’s changing climate, underpinning climate research, services and adaptation measures.
The WMO Coordination Mechanism (WCM) plays a key role in curating authoritative weather, water and climate information from the WMO Community to the United Nations and humanitarian agencies, thereby enhancing preparedness and early response efforts. Through the Early Warnings for All Initiative (EW4All), the WCM supports crisis-prone and conﬂict-affected regions with timely expert advice.
Geospatial Data and Technology While the WMO Secretariat facilitates the free exchange of data and information, the infrastructure, systems and facilities needed for the provision of these services are owned, implemented and operated by Member States and Territories.
The WMO Secretariat makes available speciﬁc observation and forecast products, data and metadata (see relevant links).
Geospatial Usage WMO monitors and analyses the coverage and conditions of the core activities described above. 81 SPECIALIZED AGENCIES Geospatial Resources The WMO Secretariat uses a mix of commercial (Esri) and open-source tools such as QGIS, PostGIS and Python to manage and make available geospatial information.

” OTHER RELATED ORGANIZATIONS 5 86 BLUEPRINT 2.0 GEOSPATIAL LANDSCAPE OF THE UNITED NATIONS SYSTEM Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty Organization (CTBTO) Geospatial Activities Acquisition and processing of geospatial information permitted under the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty Organization (CTBTO) veriﬁcation regime to ensure that no nuclear explosion can go undetected.
Geospatial Data and Technology The Treaty’s comprehensive veriﬁcation regime consists of three components: 1. The International Monitoring System (IMS) is a global network using four state-of-the-art technologies: seismic (to monitor shockwaves through the ground), hydroacoustic (to detect sound waves in the oceans), infrasound (to listen for ultra-low-frequency sound waves inaudible to the human ear) and radionuclide (to monitor the atmosphere for radioactive particles and gases from a nuclear explosion). 2. The International Data Centre (IDC), located at the CTBTO’s headquarters in Vienna, receives data from the IMS facilities. It applies both automatic processing methods and interactive human analysis to produce standard IDC products on behalf of States Parties. The IDC provides States Parties with open and equal access to raw or processed IMS data and to all IDC products, including the results of analysis conducted at certiﬁed radionuclide laboratories. 3. On-site inspection (OSI) is the ﬁnal component of the CTBT veriﬁcation regime. As part of an OSI, a range of techniques and activities, permitted under the Treaty, may be used to gather data. These data inherently have a spatial component and are processed and visualised using a combination of off-the-shelf and custom applications. The CTBT speciﬁes inspection activities and techniques that may be applied during an on-site inspection. Geospatial Usage Beyond the core purpose of detecting nuclear explosions, IMS data yield a range of wider beneﬁts that support life-saving actions and advance scientiﬁc knowledge. For example:  National tsunami warning centres in Member States can receive data in near-real-time to support faster, more accurate public alerts.  IMS radionuclide stations can contribute to the international response to a nuclear emergency by tracking the movement of harmful radionuclides.  Researchers can access selected data through the CTBTO’s Virtual Data Exploitation Centre (vDEC) programme to better understand the natural world, from whale behaviour to climate change to the timing of monsoon rains. 87 OTHER RELATED ORGANIZATIONS Geospatial Resources A range of off-the-shelf and custom applications are used to process and visualise geospatial information. 88 BLUEPRINT 2.0 GEOSPATIAL LANDSCAPE OF THE UNITED NATIONS SYSTEM International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) Geospatial Activities The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) is the world’s central intergovernmental forum for scientiﬁc and technical cooperation in the nuclear ﬁeld. It works for the safe, secure and peaceful uses of nuclear science and technology, contributing to international peace and security and the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals. As part of its mission, the IAEA independently veriﬁes that nuclear facilities are not misused and that nuclear materials remain committed to peaceful purposes. Geospatial information plays a crucial role in supporting this mission. Following the discovery of Iraq’s clandestine nuclear weapons program and North Korea’s noncompliance with safeguards obligations in the early 1990s, IAEA Member States called for enhanced measures to detect undeclared nuclear materials and activities. Since then, the IAEA has signiﬁcantly strengthened its capability to collect and analyse open-source information, including satellite imagery. This data, combined with insights from ﬁeld veriﬁcation activities, supports the IAEA in assessing the correctness and completeness of government declarations on nuclear materials. Commercial satellite imagery and derived geospatial information enable the IAEA to monitor and analyse sites of interest, especially those with restricted or challenging access due to physical or security constraints. Geospatial information is routinely used to support the following safeguarding activities:  Verifying the correctness and completeness of information supplied by governments  Supporting the planning of ﬁeld inspection activities, providing inspectors with a detailed understanding of facility infrastructure  Detecting changes and monitoring activities at sites related to the nuclear fuel cycle  Identifying potential undeclared activities Geospatial Data and Technology Data include commercially and freely available electro-optical (EO) and synthetic-aperture radar (SAR) satellite imagery; foundation geospatial datasets, including relevant vector data about nuclear fuel cycle infrastructure; georeferenced information and maps provided by governments; and a structured collection of satellite imagery observations. Technologies include desktop and web-based geographic information system (GIS) applications, geodata servers, web services and geodatabases.
Geospatial Usage The IAEA uses advanced remote sensing and GIS technologies to process and analyse geospatial data from an expanding range of remote sensing platforms and other sources. These resources provide unprecedented spatial resolution, enhanced spectral capabilities and signiﬁcantly improved revisit rates, enabling more frequent and detailed monitoring. GIS capabilities facilitate high-level storage, processing and management of satellite imagery and derived information. Through the analysis of commercial satellite imagery and the integration with other relevant information sources, the IAEA produces geospatial analytical products to support its mission.
89 OTHER RELATED ORGANIZATIONS Geospatial Resources The IAEA employs image analysts, geospatial specialists and data scientists to drive its geospatial initiatives. The Agency collects, manages and analyses geospatial data, integrating it with other information sources to produce detailed analytical products. Advanced enterprise GIS solutions support efﬁcient data storage, high-quality analytical processes and the secure dissemination of geospatial information and related products. Geospatial Representatives Representative:  Marc Laﬁtte, m.laﬁtte@iaea.org Alternative:  Milica Colakovic, m.colakovic@iaea.org Relevant Links MILESTONES IN SAFEGUARDS (IAEA.ORG) Milestones in IAEA Safeguards including Satellite Imagery analysis SG-IMPLEMENTATION-2023.PDF (IAEA.ORG) IAEA Safeguards ﬁgures including geospatial information International Organization for Migration (IOM) Geospatial Activities Geospatial tools and technology play a vital role in understanding migration and internal displacement, which are entirely based on spatial data related to locations, routes and multi-layer analysis. Geographic information system (GIS) tools have a broad range of applications for the International Organization for Migration (IOM), in particular for the Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM), which is active in 91 countries worldwide. DTM is a system developed by IOM to track and monitor population mobility and displacement. It is designed to regularly and systematically capture, process and disseminate information to provide a better understanding of the movements and evolving needs of displaced populations and migrants, whether in situ or en route. DTM is the largest source of primary data on internal displacement, consolidated at national and subnational levels. It informs 91 per cent (21 out of 23 countries) of Humanitarian Response Plans (HRPs) globally. It is formally recognized as the lead provider of countrylevel data on internal displacement in the Inter-Agency Standing Committee (IASC) Management Response to the Independent Review of the Humanitarian Response to Internal Displacement. This highlights its critical role in informing humanitarian action and ensuring that core data on internally displaced persons (IDPs) are systematically integrated into humanitarian needs assessments and response planning.
IOM’s DTM has strengthened its analytical capabilities through the application of GeoAI, machine learning, deep learning and satellite imagery, supporting:  Damage Assessment and Infrastructure Analysis: Satellite imagery combined with AI-driven damage assessment allows DTM to evaluate damage to buildings and infrastructure after disasters such as ﬂoods or cyclones. This enables efﬁcient intervention for emergency response.  Shelter Detection and Camp Mapping: Using deep learning, DTM detects and monitors shelters in camps, providing accurate shelter counts and assessing population inﬂux (with timestamps to improve tracking of population movements in sudden-onset crises). This approach tracks the expansion of camps and population movements over time.  Footprint in Urban Areas and Urban Displacement Patterns: DTM applies geospatial tools to map building footprints and monitor displaced population movements in support of data collection in large urban areas.  Emergency and Disaster Response to ﬂoods, cyclones, earthquakes and other natural disasters: DTM’s geospatial models and satellite data assess disaster impacts, such as ﬂood zones or cyclone paths, to anticipate population displacement and enhance rapid response to affected populations.  Change Detection for Monitoring Inﬂux: Through AIpowered change detection, DTM tracks shelter growth and density in displacement camps, correlating this with population inﬂux alongside ﬁeld veriﬁcation on the ground. This real-time data are essential for proactive planning and resource allocation.
These innovations support DTM’s goal of delivering accurate, timely and actionable data on displacement trends and patterns. By integrating AI-powered tools and remote sensing, United Nations agencies and the humanitarian community are better prepared to respond to complex needs in real-time and support data-driven decision-making.
Geospatial Data & Technologies In 2025, IOM’s DTM collected, analysed and disseminated data both spatial and non-spatial data on population mobility, tracking the movements of over 54.8 million IDPs and 38.4 million returnees, including 29.4 million IDP returnees and 9 million returnees from abroad. With improved geospatial analysis of displacement data, DTM published 2,158 reports and mapping products, with over 2.3 million downloads.
DTM has contributed 308 datasets to HDX, covering 33 countries. Half of these datasets include Humanitarian Exchange Language (HXL) tags, which enable faster data processing. IOM’s DTM is among the top ﬁve data providers among all United Nations organizations on HDX. This is in addition to the regular contribution to OCHA ’s Common Operational Datasets (CODs), which are authoritative reference datasets to support operations and decision-making for all actors in a humanitarian response and essential for geospatial analytics using standardized administrative boundaries. These common standardized datasets are used to improve data collection activities at country level and later at regional and global levels for data consolidation and analysis purposes. 90 BLUEPRINT 2.0 GEOSPATIAL LANDSCAPE OF THE UNITED NATIONS SYSTEM To simplify and modernize the data-sharing platform for IDPs, DTM has created a publicly accessible application programming interface (API). This API allows the humanitarian community, academia, media, government and non-governmental organizations to use data collected by DTM. As of December 2024, the DTM API was queried more than 50,000 times. The API only provides non-sensitive IDP ﬁgures, aggregated at the country, Admin 1 (states, provinces, or equivalent) and Admin 2 (smaller subnational administrative areas) levels in line with IASC Operational Guidance on Data Responsibility in Humanitarian Action guidelines.
In addition, DTM global data are available on ArcGIS Living Atlas of the World, the world’s premier collection of geographic information. This initiative marks as a signiﬁcant step in leveraging DTM global data for collaborative analysis across diverse sectors and thematic domains. Now users of GIS technologies worldwide can seamlessly integrate and analyse displacement data alongside various indicators and sectors. For instance, they can overlay displacement information with cyclone paths, hazard risks, heat waves, or vegetation changes, enabling comprehensive insights. This is in addition to the current contribution to the One UN Geospatial Situation Room, which integrates geospatial data from over 40 United Nations entities into a single interface. It provides Nexus apps that bring together data services across the thematic pillars of the United Nations for better cross-cutting knowledge and understanding of global trends. Geospatial Usage Over the years, IOM’s DTM has been progressing in line with the UN 2.0 initiative on Data, Innovation and Digital Transformation in multiple ways to adapt to rapidly changing humanitarian contexts and to support effective response and policymaking. The most recent key innovative and technological advancements in IOM’s DTM are:  Advanced Geospatial Analytics: Incorporating satellite imagery, geospatial analytics and GeoAI tools enables more accurate data on population movement, even in areas that are hard to access. DTM often combines this with remote sensing data to reﬁne the geographical accuracy of displacement patterns.  DTM Data Kit is a set of tools designed to facilitate data collection for DTM country operations and to support the global consolidation of DTM data.  DTM API accelerates secure sharing of data on internal displacement, simplifying access to data across users and partners to support action, insight and foresight.  Big Data and Predictive Analytics: By integrating predictive analytics and machine learning, DTM has started to analyse trends over time to forecast potential displacement crises, assisting preparedness and anticipatory action efforts.
Geospatial Resources DTM operates with more than 12,000 data collectors and over 500 technical experts across 91 countries. Geospatial tasks are led by dedicated GIS experts, with additional support provided by regional and global teams where needed, including deployments for emergency response and capacity-building initiatives.

91 OTHER RELATED ORGANIZATIONS 92 BLUEPRINT 2.0 GEOSPATIAL LANDSCAPE OF THE UNITED NATIONS SYSTEM International Seabed Authority (ISA) Geospatial Activities In accordance with the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) and the 1994 Agreement relating to the implementation of Part XI of the Convention (1994 Agreement), the ISA is the organization through which the States Parties to UNCLOS organize and control mineral exploration and exploitation activities in the Area, particularly with a view to administering the mineral resources of the Area, for the beneﬁt of humankind as a whole. The Convention deﬁnes “the Area” as “the seabed and ocean ﬂoor and subsoil thereof, beyond the limits of national jurisdiction” . The establishment of the exact geographic limits of the Area depends on the establishment by States of the outer limits of the continental shelf, including the delineation of the outer limits of the continental shelf, where it extends beyond 200 nautical miles from the baselines from which the breadth of the territorial sea is measured, in accordance with the Convention. Pursuant to article 84, paragraph 2, of the Convention, coastal States are obliged to give due publicity to charts or lists of geographical coordinates of points and, in the case of those indicating the outer limit lines of the continental shelf, to deposit a copy of such charts or lists with the Secretary-General of the Authority. The ISA Secretariat began to assemble and digitize historical data into its database from 2000 onward with the aim of:  Improving ISA data management through clear principles, objectives and processes governing data use;  Conducting data standardization and quality control through reporting and metadata templates based on contractor guidance for annual reports;  Migrating historical contractor data into internationally standardized digital and georeferenced formats for compatibility with other databases worldwide; and  Undertaking data governance initiatives to ensure data standardization, storage and accessibility while maintaining conﬁdentiality and security.
The ISA database was launched in July 2019 under the name “DeepData” (http://data.isa.org.jm). DeepData is an integrated database system designed to serve as a geospatial data management system. The ISA Assembly adopted an Action Plan for Marine Scientiﬁc Research to support the United Nations Decade of Ocean Science for Sustainable Development (MSR Action Plan) in 2020. The MSR Action Plan has served as a global framework and agenda to advance deep-sea research. A key aspect of the MSR Action Plan is the implementation of strategic research priorities that aim to promote the dissemination, exchange and sharing of scientiﬁc data and deep-sea research outputs and to increase deep-sea literacy. The strategic roadmap for the data management also links to other strategic research priorities:  Advancing scientiﬁc knowledge and understanding of deep-sea ecosystems, including biodiversity and ecosystem functions, in the Area  Standardizing and innovating methodologies for deep-sea biodiversity assessment, including taxonomic identiﬁcation and description, in the Area  Facilitating technology development for activities in the Area, including ocean observation and monitoring  Enhancing scientiﬁc knowledge and understanding of potential impacts of activities in the Area  Promoting dissemination, exchange and sharing of scientiﬁc data and deep-sea research outputs and increasing deep-sea literacy The importance of ocean data has also been increasingly highlighted at the international level. In 2017 , the United Nations General Assembly proclaimed the Decade of Ocean Science (2021-2030) to stimulate interdisciplinary ocean research and promote the generation and dissemination of data, information and knowledge to support the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. Geospatial Data and Technology The ISA has entered into 31 contracts involving 22 contractors for the exploration for polymetallic nodules (19 contracts) in the Clarion-Clipperton Fracture Zone (CCZ), Northwest Paciﬁc Ocean (NPO) and Central Indian Ocean Basin (CIOB); polymetallic sulphides (7 contracts) in the 93 OTHER RELATED ORGANIZATIONS CIOB; and cobalt-rich ferromanganese crusts (5 contracts) in the NPO and South Atlantic Ocean of the deep seabed. The contractors are required to submit metadata and results of sample analyses from exploration surveys in contract areas, using the digital reporting templates recommended by the Legal and Technical Commission (ISBA/21/LTC/15, Reporting Template: https://isa.org.jm/deepdata-database/ reporting-templates/ The environmental data in DeepData, including biological, physical and geochemical parameters of the marine ecosystems, are accessible to the public. The geological data relating to mineral resource assessment are formally identiﬁed as conﬁdential by the regulations on prospecting and exploration of mineral resources and are made accessible only to authorized users of ISA organs and contractors. (ISBA/19/A/9, ISBA/19/C/17 , ISBA/16/A/12/ Rev.1 and ISBA/18/A/11). The contractors are also required to produce Geographic Information System regional maps with high-resolution bathymetry showing major geological and geomorphological features, at a scale appropriate to the resource and habitat variability (ISBA/25/LTC/6). The collected bathymetric data are submitted as digital ‘xyz’ ﬁles in American Standard Code for Information Interchange (ASCII) format or a geographic information system (GIS) format. The processing sequence must be fully described (ISBA/21/LTC/15). While resource-related data, including bathymetric information, are conﬁdential, the ISA Secretariat launched the AREA2030 initiative for mapping of the ocean area by 2030. As the ﬁrst UN agency to contribute to the Ocean Biodiversity Information System (OBIS), ISA enhances global access to oceanographic data through its DeepData database in collaboration with IOC/UNESCO. Its 2011 memorandum of understanding emphasizes data sharing, enabling signiﬁcant public access to deep-sea datasets, including physical and chemical oceanographic data. In line with ISA ’s regulatory framework, environmental data from exploration activities are made publicly available, supporting marine scientiﬁc research. With over 60,000 species occurrence records, ISA DeepData plays a vital role in advancing understanding of deep-sea biodiversity and sustainable seabed knowledge. Geospatial Usage The environmental data compiled and contained in DeepData are analysed and synthesized to support (ISA) developing Regional Environmental Management Plans (REMPs) and facilitating scientiﬁc discussions that inform decision-making. The ISA Secretariat has made signiﬁcant efforts to enhance accessibility to DeepData, in alignment with the FAIR principles. This initiative aims to integrate DeepData with other public datasets, thereby supporting marine scientiﬁc research conducted by external experts and used by various research institutions. Geospatial Resources The International Seabed Authority includes one full-time geospatial expert, two staff members working with geospatial technology (professional and general service) and three scientiﬁc experts supporting geospatial data analysis and visualisation. There are 197 Parties to the Convention, including 196 country Parties and the European Union. The Convention, based on the principles of participation, partnership and decentralization, is a multilateral commitment to mitigate the impact of land degradation and protect our land to provide food, water, shelter and economic opportunity to all people. The UNCCD Permanent Secretariat is located in Bonn, Germany.
UNCCD’s geospatial activities comprise ﬁve main areas: 1) Leveraging geospatial data for monitoring and reporting on Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) Indicator 15.3.1; 2) Using open-source geospatial technology for the national reporting platform and other information tools; 3) Harnessing third-party open-source geospatial software to build the capacity of countries to use geospatial information to achieve Land Degradation Neutrality; 4) Using UN Map services to align with UN standards; and 5) Engaging with the Group on Earth Observations (GEO) through its Land Degradation Neutrality Flagship (GEO-LDN).
Geospatial Data and Technology The UNCCD national reporting platform, the Performance Review and Assessment of Implementation System (PRAIS), enables countries to report on the status and trends in land degradation and drought using geospatial information. PRAIS has an in-built web geographic information system (GIS) platform based on open GIS libraries and tools, which can handle vector and raster ﬁle formats, includes basic digitization tools and is interoperable with a QGIS plugin (Trends.Earth). While PRAIS is only accessible to accredited national reporting ofﬁcers, the publicly accessible UNCCD Data Dashboard displays the results of the reporting process in a series of maps, charts and graphs.
To manage the Land Degradation Neutrality target-setting process, the UNCCD has developed the LDN Target Tracking Tool, a knowledge management tool for LDN targets set by countries and the actions implemented to achieve them. Countries are strongly encouraged to submit geospatial information to support their targets. The tool allows searching and editing of attributes for LDN targets and visualising where targets and implemented actions are located on a map viewer. The UNCCD also hosts a map platform to visualise drought risk and sand and dust storms. This is a Java application using GeoServer, PostgreSQL and PostGIS as a database management system.
Geospatial Usage While the UNCCD Secretariat does not directly produce geospatial information, it strongly promotes the use of geospatial information and monitoring methods among its country Parties. For example, it has published a good practice guidance document to help countries use geospatial information and tools to plan and assess progress towards the SDG Target 15.3 (Land Degradation Neutrality (LDN) by 2030), including setting baselines and targets. While most countries use moderate-resolution satellite-derived information (250 m to 1 km) for this purpose, small island developing States in particular require access to high-resolution data (10 m to 30 m resolution) and the computing power and resources to manage the processing and interpretation of results.
Before the launch of every reporting process, the UNCCD Secretariat, with the assistance of its partners, collates a number of free and open global satellite-derived datasets on land cover, land productivity and soil organic carbon, processes the data and clips them to the UN Map country boundaries. Countries then access these datasets for free in the UNCCD reporting platform and can either replace them with better national data or submit them as part of their ofﬁcial national reports on SDG Indicator 15.3.1. The UNCCD also uses the United Nations Clear Map service and ofﬁcial United Nations map guidance to ensure consistent depiction of boundaries and application of required disclaimers in web and printed maps.

Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu on Wednesday said no casualties had been reported so far due to Cyclone Arnab, crediting advance precautionary measures taken by the administration.

During a teleconference with 32,000 personnel, including district collectors, Naidu directed officials to minimise property damage and restore normalcy in affected areas at the earliest.
